People Who Never Reached Age 62

Ernest Hemingway

Birth date: July 20, 1899

Death date: July 1, 1961

Age: 61

Ernest Hemingway was an American novelist, short-story writer, and journalist whose spare, forceful prose reshaped 20th-century fiction. A central voice of the Lost Generation, he wrote classics such as The Sun Also Rises, A Farewell to Arms, For Whom the Bell Tolls, and The Old Man and the Sea, winning the Pulitzer Prize and the 1954 Nobel Prize in Literature. His public image mixed literary discipline with travel, war reporting, fishing, hunting, and danger. After years of injuries, declining health, depression, and treatment, Hemingway died by suicide at his home in Ketchum, Idaho, on July 2, 1961, aged 61.

Li Bai

Birth date: May 22, 701

Death date: December 3, 762

Age: 61

Li Bai, also known as Li Po or Taibai, was one of the greatest poets of China’s Tang dynasty, celebrated for dazzling verse about friendship, nature, solitude, travel, wine, and the freedom of the imagination. A restless wanderer and brief court favorite, he became a lasting symbol of poetic genius. He died in 762 at Dangtu, probably after serious illness, though later legend turned his death into the famous story that he drowned while drunkenly trying to embrace the moon’s reflection.

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

Birth date: August 26, 1770

Death date: November 13, 1831

Age: 61

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel was a German philosopher and one of the central figures of German idealism, famous for his ambitious system of thought, his account of history as rational development, and works such as Phenomenology of Spirit and Science of Logic. He taught at Berlin and profoundly influenced philosophy, politics, theology, and social theory. He died in Berlin on 14 November 1831 at age 61, during a cholera epidemic; cholera was reported as the cause, though later accounts have questioned whether another gastrointestinal illness may have been involved.

Adolf Hitler

Birth date: April 19, 1889

Death date: April 29, 1945

Age: 56
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Extremely controversial because he was the Nazi dictator whose regime initiated the Second World War in Europe and carried out the Holocaust and other mass murders, persecutions, and aggressive wars.

Adolf Hitler was an Austrian-born German politician, leader of the Nazi Party, and dictator of Germany from 1933 to 1945. His regime launched the Second World War in Europe and was central to the Holocaust, the genocide of about six million Jews and millions of other victims. In April 1945, with Berlin surrounded by Soviet forces and Nazi Germany collapsing, Hitler withdrew into the Führerbunker and died by suicide on 30 April 1945, aged 56.

William Shakespeare

Birth date: April 22, 1564

Death date: April 22, 1616

Age: 52

William Shakespeare was an English playwright, poet, and actor from Stratford-upon-Avon, celebrated as the leading dramatist of the English language. His plays, sonnets, and narrative poems shaped world literature and theatre for centuries. He died in Stratford on 23 April 1616, traditionally his 52nd birthday; the precise cause of death is not known, though he was buried two days later at Holy Trinity Church.

Michael Jackson

Birth date: August 28, 1958

Death date: June 24, 2009

Age: 50
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Michael Jackson is highly controversial because of repeated allegations of child sexual abuse, major criminal and civil proceedings, and later documentary accounts that kept public debate active after his death. He was acquitted in his 2005 criminal trial and denied the allegations, so the controversy includes both serious accusations and disputed legal/public interpretations.

Michael Jackson was an American singer, songwriter, dancer, and global pop icon whose music, videos, choreography, and style reshaped popular entertainment. From his childhood with the Jackson 5 to solo milestones such as Off the Wall, Thriller, Bad, and Dangerous, he became one of the best-selling and most influential performers in history. He died in Los Angeles on June 25, 2009, at age 50, from cardiac arrest linked to acute propofol and sedative intoxication while preparing for his This Is It concert series.

Birth date: February 11, 1809

Death date: April 14, 1865

Age: 56

Abraham Lincoln was the 16th president of the United States, a self-educated lawyer and Republican leader who guided the Union through the Civil War and became central to the abolition of slavery. He was shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford’s Theatre on April 14, 1865, and died the next morning in Washington, D.C.

Vladimir Lenin

Birth date: April 21, 1870

Death date: January 20, 1924

Age: 53
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Lenin is highly controversial because he founded and led a one-party revolutionary state, used political repression against opponents, and is associated with the Red Terror, civil-war coercion, censorship, and the creation of institutions that shaped later Soviet authoritarianism.

Vladimir Lenin, born Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov, was a Russian revolutionary, Marxist theorist, founder of the Bolshevik faction, and the first head of government of Soviet Russia and later the Soviet Union. He led the October Revolution of 1917 and shaped the one-party Soviet state through policies including nationalization, civil-war centralization, and the New Economic Policy. After a series of debilitating strokes in 1922 and 1923, Lenin’s health collapsed; he died at Gorki on 21 January 1924 at the age of 53.

Julius Caesar

Birth date: July 11, 100 BCE

Death date: March 14, 44 BCE

Age: 55
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Julius Caesar is controversial as a conqueror and authoritarian political leader. His campaigns in Gaul caused mass death, enslavement, and displacement, and his crossing of the Rubicon, civil war, and dictatorship helped destroy the Roman Republic.

Julius Caesar was a Roman general, statesman and author whose conquest of Gaul, alliance with Pompey and Crassus, victory in civil war and dictatorship reshaped the Roman Republic and helped prepare the Roman Empire. After accepting the title dictator for life in 44 BC, he was stabbed to death by a senatorial conspiracy led by Brutus and Cassius on the Ides of March, an assassination that triggered another round of civil wars.

Ludwig van Beethoven

Birth date: December 15, 1770

Death date: March 25, 1827

Age: 56

Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist whose music helped drive the transition from the Classical era to Romanticism. Born in Bonn and later based in Vienna, he transformed the symphony, sonata, concerto, and string quartet, creating works such as the Fifth and Ninth Symphonies, Fidelio, the late piano sonatas, and the late quartets. His growing deafness made his career even more extraordinary. After several months of serious illness marked by symptoms such as jaundice, swelling, and abdominal fluid, he died in Vienna on 26 March 1827 at the age of 56.

Dante Alighieri

Birth date: May 31, 1265

Death date: September 13, 1321

Age: 56

Dante Alighieri was a Florentine poet, political exile, philosopher, and author of the Divine Comedy, one of the defining works of world literature and a cornerstone of the Italian language. Banished from Florence in 1302, he spent his later life moving between Italian courts and completed his masterpiece in exile. He died in Ravenna in September 1321, aged 56, most likely from malaria contracted after returning from a diplomatic mission to Venice.

Fyodor Dostoyevsky

Birth date: November 10, 1821

Death date: February 8, 1881

Age: 59

Fyodor Dostoevsky was a Russian novelist, journalist and thinker whose psychological fiction reshaped world literature. His major works include Crime and Punishment, The Idiot, Demons and The Brothers Karamazov, novels famous for their moral intensity, spiritual conflict and unforgettable characters. In his final days in Saint Petersburg, he suffered repeated pulmonary hemorrhages; after a last decline at home, he died on 9 February 1881 at the age of 59.

Napoleon

Birth date: August 14, 1769

Death date: May 4, 1821

Age: 51
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Napoleon is highly controversial because his rule combined major legal and administrative reforms with authoritarian government, censorship, dynastic ambition, and years of large-scale war across Europe. His 1802 restoration of slavery in French colonies and the violent campaigns of the Napoleonic era are central reasons his legacy is disputed.

Napoleon Bonaparte, later Napoleon I, was a Corsican-born French general and statesman who rose during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French. He reshaped Europe through military campaigns, state reforms, and the Napoleonic Code, leaving a legacy admired for administrative modernization and criticized for war, authoritarian rule, and the restoration of slavery in French colonies. After his defeat at Waterloo, he was exiled to Saint Helena, where his health declined. He died at Longwood House on 5 May 1821, aged 51, most commonly attributed to stomach cancer.

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk

Birth date: May 18, 1881

Death date: November 9, 1938

Age: 57

Mustafa Kemal Atatürk was the Ottoman-born soldier, statesman, and reformer who founded the Republic of Turkey and served as its first president from 1923 to 1938. A commander at Gallipoli and leader of the Turkish War of Independence, he reshaped the new republic through secular, legal, educational, linguistic, and cultural reforms. In his final year his health declined from liver disease, commonly identified as cirrhosis; he died at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul on 10 November 1938, aged 57.

Charles Dickens

Birth date: February 6, 1812

Death date: June 8, 1870

Age: 58

Charles Dickens was one of the defining writers of Victorian Britain, famous for novels such as Oliver Twist, David Copperfield, A Christmas Carol, Bleak House, A Tale of Two Cities, and Great Expectations. A former journalist and tireless public reader, he turned social injustice, poverty, childhood hardship, and urban life into unforgettable fiction. In his final years, heavy work and public readings strained his health; after suffering a final stroke at Gad's Hill Place in Kent, he died the next day on 9 June 1870, aged 58, leaving The Mystery of Edwin Drood unfinished.

Friedrich Nietzsche

Birth date: October 14, 1844

Death date: August 24, 1900

Age: 55

Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche was a German philosopher, classical philologist, poet, and cultural critic whose work reshaped modern thought through ideas such as perspectivism, the critique of morality, the death of God, eternal recurrence, and the Übermensch. A former professor at Basel, he became an independent writer after years of illness. In 1889 he suffered a severe mental collapse and spent his final years incapacitated under family care. After strokes and pneumonia in 1900, he died in Weimar at the age of 55.

René Descartes

Birth date: March 30, 1596

Death date: February 10, 1650

Age: 53

René Descartes was a French philosopher, mathematician, and scientist whose method of radical doubt and famous idea “I think, therefore I am” helped shape modern philosophy. He also linked algebra and geometry, giving his name to Cartesian coordinates. In 1649 he moved to Stockholm to tutor Queen Christina of Sweden; the cold climate, early-morning lessons, and illness are traditionally connected with the pneumonia that led to his death on 11 February 1650, at age 53.

Christopher Columbus

Birth date: October 30, 1451

Death date: May 19, 1506

Age: 54
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Christopher Columbus is highly controversial because his voyages are tied to European colonization of the Americas, Indigenous dispossession, forced labor, enslavement, violence, and catastrophic population loss. He is also criticized for his conduct as governor in the Caribbean and for becoming a symbol in modern debates over conquest and colonial memory.

Christopher Columbus was a Genoese navigator and explorer whose four Spanish-sponsored Atlantic voyages transformed European knowledge of the Americas and helped launch a long era of exploration, conquest, and colonization. Ambitious, skilled, and controversial, he sought a westward route to Asia but reached Caribbean lands instead. After years of illness, disputes over titles and revenues, and declining royal favor, he died in Valladolid, Spain, on 20 May 1506, still convinced he had reached the fringes of Asia. He was 54.

Niccolò Machiavelli

Birth date: May 2, 1469

Death date: June 20, 1527

Age: 58

Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat, political thinker, historian, playwright, and author whose sharp analysis of power made The Prince one of the most influential political books ever written. He served the Florentine Republic during a turbulent Renaissance era of shifting alliances, Medici rule, and foreign invasion. After losing office, he wrote the works that made his name synonymous with hard-headed political realism. He died near Florence in 1527, aged 58, after suffering from a stomach illness; he received last rites and was later buried in the Basilica of Santa Croce.

Death date: October 4, 2011

Age: 56

Steve Jobs was an American entrepreneur, inventor, and investor who co-founded Apple, helped shape the personal-computer revolution, built NeXT, and played a major role in Pixar’s rise. Known for his intense product vision, he helped bring the Macintosh, iPod, iPhone, and iPad into popular culture. He died at his home in Palo Alto on October 5, 2011, from complications related to a previously treated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, after years of serious health problems.

Benito Mussolini

Birth date: July 28, 1883

Death date: April 27, 1945

Age: 61
Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Mussolini is one of the most controversial figures in modern history. He founded Fascism, ruled Italy as a dictator, suppressed political opposition, used state violence, pursued imperial wars, enacted antisemitic racial laws, allied with Nazi Germany, and helped lead Italy into World War II.

Benito Mussolini was an Italian politician, journalist, and dictator who founded Fascism and ruled Italy as Il Duce from 1922 until his overthrow in 1943. He turned Italy into a one-party dictatorship, aligned with Nazi Germany, and led the country into World War II. After the collapse of his regime, he tried to flee northern Italy with Clara Petacci, but was captured by Italian partisans and summarily executed on 1945-04-28 at age 61.

Virgil, born Publius Vergilius Maro, was the great Roman poet of the Augustan age and the author of the Eclogues, the Georgics, and the Aeneid, the epic that became a cornerstone of Latin literature. In 19 BC, after meeting Augustus in Athens and traveling in Greece, he fell ill, returned to Italy, and died at Brundisium before finishing the Aeneid; Augustus ordered the poem preserved rather than burned.

Ovid, born Publius Ovidius Naso, was one of the great poets of Augustan Rome, celebrated for the Metamorphoses, Ars Amatoria, Amores, Heroides, Fasti, and his elegant mastery of myth, love poetry, and transformation. In 8 CE Augustus exiled him to Tomis on the Black Sea for what Ovid famously called a carmen et error, “a poem and a mistake.” He spent his final years pleading to return to Rome, but died in exile at about 59.

James Joyce was an Irish novelist, poet, and literary critic whose daring experiments with language helped define literary modernism. His major works include Dubliners, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, Ulysses, and Finnegans Wake. After years of poor health and exile across continental Europe, he died in Zürich on 13 January 1941 following surgery for a perforated duodenal ulcer. He was 58.

Theodore Roosevelt

Birth date: October 26, 1858

Age: 60

Theodore Roosevelt Jr. was the 26th president of the United States, a reform-minded Republican, conservationist, writer, soldier, and Nobel Peace Prize laureate. Famous for his energetic public life, the Rough Riders, antitrust campaigns, and the expansion of national parks and federal power, he became one of the defining figures of the Progressive Era. After years of physical strain and illness, he died in his sleep at Sagamore Hill, Oyster Bay, on January 6, 1919, from an embolism or blood clot-related heart event.

Herodotus

Birth date: December 31, 484 BCE

Death date: December 31, 425 BCE

Age: 59

Herodotus was a Greek historian and geographer from Halicarnassus, best known for the Histories, his wide-ranging account of the Greco-Persian Wars, imperial power, travel, customs, and storytelling across the ancient Mediterranean and Near East. Cicero later called him the “Father of History,” a title that reflects both his ambition and his lasting influence. He appears to have died around 425 BCE, probably in late middle age, with ancient tradition associating his final years with Thurii in southern Italy or, less certainly, Pella in Macedon. No reliable account preserves the cause of his death, so his age at death is best estimated as 59.

Molière, born Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, was the towering comic playwright, actor, and theatre director of 17th-century France, famous for Tartuffe, The Misanthrope, The School for Wives, and The Imaginary Invalid. His sharp satire of hypocrisy, pretension, medicine, marriage, and social vanity made him a central figure in French literature. Already weakened by illness, he collapsed after performing as Argan in The Imaginary Invalid and died in Paris a few hours later, aged 51.

Age: 60
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Leon Trotsky is highly controversial because he was a leading Bolshevik revolutionary and commander of the Red Army during a period of civil war, political repression, executions, and authoritarian consolidation in the early Soviet state.

Leon Trotsky, born Lev Davidovich Bronstein, was a Russian revolutionary, Marxist theorist, Soviet politician, and one of the central figures of the 1917 Russian Revolution and the early Soviet state. A founder and commander of the Red Army, he later lost the power struggle with Joseph Stalin, was expelled from the Soviet Union, and spent his final years in exile. In Mexico City, after surviving an earlier attack, he was fatally wounded by Ramón Mercader, an assassin linked to Soviet intelligence, and died the next day at age 60.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Hugo Chávez is highly controversial because his presidency combined mass popular support with accusations of authoritarianism, concentration of executive power, pressure on independent media, politicization of state institutions, hostility toward opponents, and economic policies widely linked by critics to Venezuela's later crisis.

Hugo Rafael Chávez Frías was a Venezuelan military officer and politician who served as president of Venezuela from 1999 until 2013, reshaping the country through his Bolivarian Revolution, socialist policies, anti-U.S. rhetoric, and deep appeal among poorer Venezuelans. After nearly two years of treatment for cancer, including surgeries in Cuba and complications from his illness, he died in Caracas on 2013-03-05 at the age of 58.

Johannes Kepler

Birth date: December 26, 1571

Death date: November 14, 1630

Age: 58

Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer, mathematician, astrologer, and natural philosopher whose laws of planetary motion transformed astronomy and helped lay the foundations of modern science. He worked with Tycho Brahe, served as imperial mathematician, and wrote influential works including Astronomia nova, Harmonice Mundi, and the Rudolphine Tables. In 1630 he traveled to Regensburg to pursue unpaid imperial salary claims, fell ill after arriving, and died there on 15 November at age 58.

Anton Pavlovich Chekhov was a Russian playwright, short-story writer, and physician whose spare, psychologically subtle style helped reshape modern drama and fiction. His major plays include The Seagull, Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, and The Cherry Orchard, while his stories remain landmarks of literary realism. Long ill with tuberculosis, he traveled to Badenweiler, Germany, seeking relief; he died there on 15 July 1904 at the age of 44 after years of declining health.

Diego Armando Maradona was an Argentine football player and manager, celebrated as one of the greatest and most charismatic figures in the history of the sport. A gifted number 10 known for extraordinary dribbling, vision, leadership, and improvisation, he inspired Argentina to victory at the 1986 FIFA World Cup and became a legend at clubs including Boca Juniors, Barcelona, and Napoli. Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose bold colour, expressive brushwork and emotional intensity helped shape modern art. Although he worked seriously as an artist for only about a decade, he produced masterpieces including Sunflowers, The Starry Night and many self-portraits. Andy Warhol

Death date: February 21, 1987

Age: 58

Andy Warhol was an American artist, filmmaker, publisher, and leading figure of Pop art, famous for turning consumer products, celebrities, advertising, and mass media into bold visual icons. Works such as Campbell’s Soup Cans, Marilyn Diptych, and his celebrity silkscreens reshaped modern ideas of art, fame, repetition, and commercial culture. He also made experimental films, founded Interview magazine, and became a central figure in New York’s avant-garde scene. Warhol died in New York City on February 22, 1987, at age 58, from complications after gallbladder surgery, commonly reported as cardiac arrhythmia following the operation.

Age: 56

Albrecht Dürer was the defining artist of the German Renaissance: a painter, engraver, printmaker, and theorist whose woodcuts, engravings, portraits, and studies of proportion carried his reputation across Europe. He worked from Nuremberg, travelled to Italy and the Low Countries, and became admired by artists and patrons far beyond Germany. After returning from the Netherlands in 1521, he suffered years of failing health and produced less art while focusing on theoretical writings. He died in Nuremberg on 6 April 1528, aged 56, and was buried in the Johannisfriedhof cemetery.

Virginia Woolf was an English novelist, essayist, publisher, and critic, widely regarded as one of the defining modernist writers of the 20th century. After years of recurring mental illness and amid the strain of wartime Britain, she died by suicide on 28 March 1941, drowning in the River Ouse near her home in Sussex.

He led the first successful expedition through the Northwest Passage and, in 1911, became the first person to reach the South Pole. In June 1928, he disappeared in the Arctic while flying a rescue mission for the crashed Italia airship; wreckage was later found, but his body was never recovered.

Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and one of history’s best-known Stoic philosophers, remembered for the Meditations and for ruling during the later Pax Romana. His reign was marked by war on the empire’s frontiers, plague, administrative pressure, and the challenge of preserving Roman stability. He died aged 58 while on campaign in the Danubian region, probably at Vindobona or near Sirmium, of unknown causes; later tradition often associates the period with the Antonine Plague.

He brought Russian music to an international audience while blending Western conservatory technique with a deeply personal expressive style. He died in Saint Petersburg on 6 November 1893, aged 53. His death is traditionally attributed to cholera and its complications, though later speculation about suicide has remained controversial and is not supported by firm documentary evidence.

After imprisonment and exile, his health declined; he died in Paris on 30 November 1900 from meningitis, commonly linked to an ear infection, at the age of 46.

In his final years, he broadened his work to address poverty and opposition to the Vietnam War. King was assassinated on April 4, 1968, in Memphis, Tennessee, while supporting striking sanitation workers and preparing the Poor People’s Campaign. He died at the age of 39.

Matsuo Bashō was the great Edo-period Japanese poet who transformed haikai and later became celebrated as the supreme master of haiku. Born near Ueno in Iga Province, he built a life around teaching, travel, literary experiment, and sharply observed scenes of nature and impermanence. His travel writing, especially the journey associated with The Narrow Road to the Deep North, helped make wandering itself part of his artistic legend. In 1694, while traveling again, Bashō fell ill in Osaka, apparently from a stomach ailment, and died there on November 28 at about age 50, surrounded by the aura of the road that had shaped his poetry.

His final years were marked by severe illness and confinement to what he called his “mattress-grave”; he died in Paris on 17 February 1856 at the age of 58 and was buried in Montmartre Cemetery.

He died in 1924 at a sanatorium near Vienna after tuberculosis, especially affecting his throat, made eating extremely painful; he was 40 years old.

Calvin Coolidge was the 30th president of the United States, serving from 1923 to 1929 after first rising through Massachusetts politics as a lawyer, governor, and vice president. After leaving office, he returned to Northampton, Massachusetts, wrote and spoke publicly, and lived a comparatively quiet retirement. He died suddenly at home on January 5, 1933, from coronary thrombosis, a form of heart-related clotting, at the age of 60.

George Orwell, born Eric Arthur Blair, was an English novelist, essayist, journalist, and critic whose clear prose and fierce opposition to totalitarianism made him one of the defining political writers of the twentieth century. His final years were marked by severe tuberculosis; after completing Nineteen Eighty-Four, he was treated in hospital in London, where he died from the disease on 21 January 1950 at the age of 46.

After the First World War, he advised on Germany’s new constitutional order and returned to teaching in Munich. He died there on 14 June 1920 at age 56, from pneumonia often linked to the influenza pandemic, leaving major work unfinished.

Ali ibn Abi Talib was a central figure in early Islam: cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad, husband of Fatima, fourth Rashidun caliph, and the first Imam in Shia tradition. Revered for his piety, legal judgment, eloquence, and courage, he became caliph in 656 during a period of deep political conflict after the murder of Uthman. His rule was marked by civil war and disputes over legitimate leadership. In January 661, he was struck with a poison-coated sword by the Kharijite Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam while at or entering the mosque in Kufa, and died from the wound shortly afterward.

Alexander the Great, king of Macedon and one of antiquity’s most influential commanders, inherited the throne at 20 and built an empire stretching from Greece through Egypt and Persia toward northwestern India. Undefeated in battle, he spread Greek political and cultural influence across much of the ancient world. He died in Babylon in June 323 BCE after a sudden illness, before securing a clear succession, leaving his empire to fragment among his generals. He was 32.

Qin Shi Huang

Birth date: January 31, 259 BCE

Death date: July 11, 210 BCE

Age: 49
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Qin Shi Huang was an authoritarian imperial ruler whose legacy includes wars of conquest, harsh Legalist punishments, forced labor on enormous state projects, censorship, and traditional accounts of book burning and executions of scholars. Some details of those accounts are debated, but his rule is strongly associated with coercive centralized power.

Qin Shi Huang, born Ying Zheng, was the founder of the Qin dynasty and the first emperor of a unified China. After defeating the rival Warring States, he centralized rule, standardized writing, weights, measures and coinage, expanded roads and walls, and left behind the famous mausoleum guarded by the Terracotta Army. He died in 210 BC during his fifth inspection tour of eastern China after becoming seriously ill; later tradition links his final years to an obsession with immortality, and mercury-based elixirs have often been suggested as a possible factor, though the exact cause remains uncertain.

Albert Camus was a French-Algerian writer, philosopher, journalist, playwright, and one of the defining literary voices of the twentieth century. Born in French Algeria, he became famous for works such as The Stranger, The Plague, The Myth of Sisyphus, The Fall, and The Rebel, and received the 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature. His writing explored absurdity, revolt, moral responsibility, and human dignity in a violent century. Camus died on 4 January 1960 at age 46 in a car crash near Sens, France, while traveling in a Facel Vega driven by his friend and publisher Michel Gallimard.

Long troubled by severe asthma and fragile health, he spent his final years increasingly confined while still revising his great novel. He died in Paris on 18 November 1922 from pneumonia and pulmonary complications at the age of 51.

Born into a wealthy Saudi family, he became involved in jihadist networks during the Soviet-Afghan War and later built al-Qaeda into an international terrorist movement. He died at age 54 on 2 May 2011, when U.S. Navy SEALs killed him during a raid on his compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan.

Aristophanes was the sharpest surviving voice of ancient Greek Old Comedy, an Athenian playwright whose political satire, outrageous fantasy, and verbal brilliance shaped the history of comic drama. Known for disciplined seamanship, careful mapping, and scientific observation, he became one of the most influential maritime figures of the eighteenth century. During his third voyage, a dispute at Kealakekua Bay in Hawaii escalated into violence, and Cook was killed there on 14 February 1779 at the age of 50.

Bertolt Brecht

Birth date: February 9, 1898

Death date: August 13, 1956

Age: 58

Bertolt Brecht was a German playwright, poet, theatre director, and one of the defining figures of modern drama. He reshaped 20th-century theatre through epic theatre, the alienation effect, and works such as The Threepenny Opera, Mother Courage and Her Children, and The Life of Galileo. Exiled after the Nazi rise to power, he later settled in East Berlin and co-founded the Berliner Ensemble. Brecht died in East Berlin on 14 August 1956 at the age of 58, commonly reported as the result of a heart attack after years of serious heart problems.

Heraclitus of Ephesus was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher active around 500 BCE, famous for the Logos, the unity of opposites, and the vision of reality as constant change. Enrico Fermi

Birth date: September 28, 1901

Death date: November 27, 1954

Age: 53

Enrico Fermi was an Italian-American physicist whose rare command of both theory and experiment helped shape modern nuclear and particle physics. A Nobel Prize winner in 1938, he developed key ideas in Fermi-Dirac statistics, beta decay, and neutron physics, and led the team that achieved the first controlled self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction at Chicago Pile-1. After the war he continued teaching and researching at the University of Chicago. He died in Chicago on 28 November 1954 from stomach cancer, aged 53, after an illness that cut short one of the most influential scientific careers of the twentieth century.

Death date: March 11, 1925

Age: 58

Sun Yat-sen, also known as Sun Zhongshan and Sun Wen, was a Chinese revolutionary, physician, and political leader whose work helped bring down the Qing dynasty and establish the Republic of China. He became the republic’s first provisional president in 1912 and later led the Kuomintang, earning a lasting reputation as a founding figure of modern China. In his final months he was gravely ill in Beijing; doctors found advanced cancer involving the liver, and later reassessments have pointed to gallbladder cancer that had spread. He died in Beijing on 12 March 1925 at the age of 58.

Sir Walter Scott was a Scottish novelist, poet, historian, and lawyer whose Waverley novels helped establish the historical novel as a major literary form. Works such as Ivanhoe, Waverley, Marmion, and The Lady of the Lake made him one of the most widely read writers of the nineteenth century. After years of intense work, debt, and declining health, he suffered strokes, returned from a failed restorative journey abroad, and died at his home, Abbotsford, on 21 September 1832 at the age of 61.

Honoré de Balzac was a French novelist, playwright, critic, and journalist, celebrated as one of the great founders of literary realism. After years of punishing work habits, debts, and worsening health, he married Ewelina Hańska in March 1850. He died in Paris five months later, aged 51, with medical accounts associating his death with gangrene and congestive heart failure.

George Eliot, born Mary Ann Evans, was one of the defining novelists of Victorian England, admired for the realism, moral complexity, and psychological depth of works such as Adam Bede, The Mill on the Floss, Silas Marner, Middlemarch, and Daniel Deronda. Writing under a male pen name helped her work be judged seriously in a literary culture dominated by men. After marrying John Walter Cross in 1880 and moving to Chelsea, London, she became ill with a throat infection, made worse by long-standing kidney disease, and died on 22 December 1880 at the age of 61.

Jane Austen

Death date: July 17, 1817

Age: 41

Jane Austen was an English novelist whose sharply observant fiction transformed the novel of manners and helped shape literary realism. Best known for Pride and Prejudice, Sense and Sensibility, Emma, Mansfield Park, Persuasion, and Northanger Abbey, she wrote with wit, irony, and unusual insight into class, marriage, money, and women’s limited choices in Georgian society. Her fame grew greatly after her death, and her books have remained central to English literature. In her final year she suffered a serious, poorly understood illness, moved to Winchester to seek medical help, and died there on 18 July 1817 at the age of 41; later theories have included Addison’s disease, Hodgkin lymphoma, lupus, tuberculosis, and cancer.

Gregor Johann Mendel was an Austrian Augustinian friar, teacher, botanist, meteorologist and mathematician whose pea-plant experiments in Brno laid the foundation for modern genetics. In his final years, administrative duties as abbot limited his scientific work, and after a serious illness in 1883 he died in Brno on 6 January 1884, aged 61, most often described as from chronic nephritis or kidney failure.

William McKinley was the 25th president of the United States, a Republican leader associated with protective tariffs, industrial growth, the Spanish–American War, and a major expansion of American influence overseas. His presidency ended after he was shot by anarchist Leon Czolgosz at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo on September 6, 1901; infection and gangrene set in, and he died eight days later at age 58.

Charles Baudelaire was a French poet, essayist, translator, and art critic whose Les Fleurs du mal helped reshape modern poetry with its urban intensity, musical language, and unsettling beauty. Alan Mathison Turing was an English mathematician, logician, cryptanalyst and pioneering computer scientist whose work shaped theoretical computer science, artificial intelligence and modern computing. During the Second World War he played a crucial role at Bletchley Park in breaking German ciphers, including Enigma-related naval traffic. Brilliant, principled, and deeply religious, he became one of the most famous figures of Tudor England. His downfall came when he refused to accept Henry VIII’s break with Rome and the king’s supremacy over the English Church. Convicted of treason, he was beheaded on Tower Hill in 1535 at the age of 57.

In 1871 he became the first Cavendish Professor of Physics at Cambridge. Maxwell died in Cambridge on 5 November 1879, aged 48, after suffering from abdominal or stomach cancer.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Oliver Cromwell is highly controversial because he helped overthrow and execute Charles I, ruled through military-backed authority, and led brutal campaigns in Ireland, especially at Drogheda and Wexford. His legacy is sharply divided between reformer, revolutionary, dictator, and perpetrator of severe wartime atrocities.

Oliver Cromwell was an English soldier, parliamentarian and statesman who rose from provincial gentry to become one of the central figures of the English Civil Wars. A gifted cavalry commander for Parliament, he helped defeat the royalists, supported the trial and execution of Charles I, and later ruled England, Scotland and Ireland as Lord Protector. His legacy remains fiercely debated, admired by some for religious and political reform and condemned by others for military rule and brutal campaigns, especially in Ireland. He died at Whitehall in 1658, aged 59, probably after a severe illness involving malarial fever, urinary or kidney trouble, and likely sepsis.

During World War II he flew reconnaissance missions for France. Charles V was the Habsburg ruler whose crowns linked Spain, the Low Countries, Austria, parts of Italy, and the Holy Roman Empire, creating one of the most formidable dynastic powers of the sixteenth century. As Charles I of Spain, he also ruled during the expansion of Spain’s American empire. Worn down by war, religious conflict, and chronic gout, he abdicated much of his power and retired to the Monastery of Yuste in Spain, where he became seriously ill, likely with malaria, and died in the early hours of 21 September 1558 at age 58.

John Calvin was a French theologian, pastor, lawyer, and one of the central figures of the Protestant Reformation. In his final years his health declined severely, including lung trouble and other chronic illnesses. He preached his last sermon in February 1564, said farewell to Geneva’s ministers in April, and died in Geneva on 27 May 1564 at the age of 54. Dag Hammarskjöld was a Swedish economist, diplomat, and the second Secretary-General of the United Nations, serving from 1953 until 1961. He helped define the modern role of the UN chief through preventive diplomacy, peacekeeping, and a strong belief in an independent international civil service. His work during crises in the Middle East and Congo made him one of the most respected diplomats of the twentieth century. He died at age 56 when his aircraft crashed near Ndola, Northern Rhodesia, while he was traveling to negotiate a ceasefire during the Congo Crisis; the exact circumstances of the crash have remained the subject of later inquiries.

Cleopatra

Birth date: January 12, 69 BCE

Death date: August 11, 30 BCE

Age: 39

Cleopatra VII Thea Philopator was the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt and one of antiquity’s most politically skilled monarchs. A Greek-speaking queen from the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty, she ruled Egypt during the final crisis of the Roman Republic and allied herself first with Julius Caesar and later with Mark Antony. After Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra’s forces, Antony died by suicide, and Cleopatra followed shortly afterward in Alexandria, probably by poisoning, to avoid being displayed in a Roman triumph. She was 39 years old.

Rising from Paris street singing to international stages, she became one of France’s most celebrated popular artists. After years of fragile health, addiction, and exhaustion, she died in 1963 at age 47, commonly linked to liver cancer or liver failure, and was buried at Père Lachaise Cemetery.

Alexander Pope was one of the defining English poets of the Augustan age, famous for the polished heroic couplets, sharp satire, and moral wit of An Essay on Criticism, The Rape of the Lock, The Dunciad, and his Homer translations. Catholic, largely self-educated, and chronically ill since childhood, he turned physical and social limits into literary force. His health failed in 1744; after receiving Catholic last rites, he died late at night at his Twickenham villa, surrounded by friends.

Death date: September 8, 1087

Age: 59
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: William the Conqueror is strongly controversial because his conquest of England involved invasion, mass dispossession, violent suppression of resistance, and the Harrying of the North, which caused severe devastation and famine. He is both a major state-builder and a ruler associated with conquest and harsh military rule.

William the Conqueror, also known as William I of England, was Duke of Normandy from childhood and became the first Norman king of England after defeating Harold Godwinson at the Battle of Hastings in 1066. His reign transformed English landholding, government, aristocracy, and church life, and included the Domesday Book survey. In 1087, during a campaign in northern France, he was injured or fell ill after the attack on Mantes and died at Rouen on 9 September, aged 59; his burial at Caen was famously troubled and chaotic.

She died in Los Angeles on December 27, 2016, four days after a medical emergency on a flight from London; officials cited sleep apnea and other contributing factors, including heart disease and drug use, while the exact cause could not be determined.

In his final years his health declined seriously, and after months of prolonged illness he died in Lahore on 21 April 1938 at the age of 60; his tomb stands near the Badshahi Mosque and Lahore Fort.

George VI, born Albert Frederick Arthur George, was King of the United Kingdom and the Dominions from 1936 to 1952. A reserved but dutiful monarch, he unexpectedly took the throne after the abdication of his brother Edward VIII and became a symbol of steadiness during the Second World War. He supported Britain through the Blitz, helped restore confidence in the monarchy, and was the father of Queen Elizabeth II. His later years were marked by serious smoking-related illness, including lung surgery; he died in his sleep at Sandringham on 6 February 1952, aged 56.

Death date: December 2, 1894

Age: 44

Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish novelist, poet, essayist and travel writer whose restless imagination produced Treasure Island, Kidnapped, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, and A Child's Garden of Verses. Born in Edinburgh and often weakened by chronic respiratory illness, he turned poor health and travel into literary energy, eventually settling in Samoa, where he became known as Tusitala, the teller of tales. On 3 December 1894, at his home in Vailima, he suddenly collapsed after speaking with his wife and died within hours, probably from a stroke or brain haemorrhage. He was buried on Mount Vaea overlooking the sea.

Why this is controversial: Highly controversial because he was a privateer involved in violent raids, imperial expansion, and early English slave-trading voyages. His reputation differs sharply between celebratory English naval history and perspectives that emphasize piracy, colonial violence, and slavery.

Sir Francis Drake was an English explorer, privateer, naval commander, and politician of the Elizabethan age, famed for completing the first English circumnavigation of the globe and for his role against the Spanish Armada. He was also involved in early English slaving voyages and became a feared raider of Spanish possessions. Drake died on 28 January 1596 during a failed expedition near Portobelo, Panama, most likely from dysentery, and was buried at sea in a lead-lined coffin.

Born in Becerril, Cesar, he became famous as the lead singer and co-founder, with accordionist Israel Romero, of Binomio de Oro de América, a group beloved across Colombia, Mexico, and Venezuela. His warm, lyrical style made him a lasting icon of Colombian folk-pop music. He was shot dead outside his home in Barranquilla during his daughter’s quinceañera; later accounts linked the murder to jealousy and underworld connections, though some details remain disputed.

Why this is controversial: Nicholas II of Russia is highly controversial because his reign involved autocratic rule, repression of political opposition, failures during the Russo-Japanese War, the Bloody Sunday crisis, antisemitic violence within the empire, and catastrophic wartime leadership during World War I. His execution and later canonization also make his memory politically and religiously disputed.

Nicholas II, born Nikolai Alexandrovich Romanov, was the last Emperor of Russia, ruling from 1894 until his abdication during the upheaval of 1917. His reign saw industrial growth but also deep political unrest, the Russo-Japanese War, the 1905 Revolution, and the strains of World War I. After abdicating, he and his family were held by revolutionary authorities and were executed by Bolsheviks in Yekaterinburg on 17 July 1918, ending the Romanov dynasty’s rule.

Rainer Maria Rilke was an Austrian poet and writer born in Prague, widely regarded as one of the most important German-language literary figures of the modern era. His major works include Duino Elegies, Sonnets to Orpheus, The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge, and Letters to a Young Poet. Restless and cosmopolitan, he lived and worked across Europe before spending his final years in Switzerland. He had been seriously ill for some time, and his condition was eventually diagnosed as leukemia. Rilke died at the Valmont sanatorium near Lake Geneva on 29 December 1926, aged 51.

Nikolai Gogol was a Ukrainian-born writer of the Russian Empire whose stories, plays, and novel Dead Souls reshaped Russian literature with satire, grotesque comedy, folklore, and psychological strangeness. In his final years he became increasingly religious, anxious, and physically weakened; after burning manuscripts, including material from the second part of Dead Souls, he refused food and died in Moscow at the age of 42.

Death date: December 31, 434 BCE

Age: 60

Empedocles of Acragas was a Greek pre-Socratic philosopher, poet, statesman, and religious thinker from Sicily. He is best known for teaching that the world is made from four roots—earth, water, air, and fire—moved by the opposing forces of Love and Strife. He also wrote in verse, argued against animal sacrifice, and developed ideas about reincarnation. His death was already legendary in antiquity: stories claimed he vanished, died abroad, or threw himself into Mount Etna, but the most defensible tradition says he died at about 60.

Humphrey DeForest Bogart was an American actor whose laconic style, hard-edged charisma, and unexpectedly vulnerable screen presence made him one of classic Hollywood’s defining figures. He became famous through films such as The Maltese Falcon, Casablanca, The Treasure of the Sierra Madre, The African Queen, and The Caine Mutiny, and later became a lasting symbol of film noir and wartime romance. After years of heavy smoking and declining health, he developed cancer around the esophagus. Surgery and treatment failed to stop the disease, and he died in Los Angeles on January 14, 1957, at age 57.

Jacques Offenbach was a German-born French composer, cellist, conductor, and impresario who became one of the defining figures of 19th-century operetta. Famous for works such as Orpheus in the Underworld and the unfinished opera The Tales of Hoffmann, he shaped the witty, satirical musical theatre that influenced Johann Strauss II, Franz von Suppé, and Arthur Sullivan. In his final years he suffered from severe gout and declining health while trying to complete The Tales of Hoffmann. He died in Paris on 5 October 1880, reportedly from heart failure brought on by acute gout, and was buried in Montmartre Cemetery.

Amerigo Vespucci was a Florentine merchant, navigator and explorer whose accounts of Atlantic voyages helped Europeans understand that the lands west of the ocean were not Asia but a separate New World. He died there on 22 February 1512, shortly before his 58th birthday, at age 57; some accounts connect his final decline with repeated bouts of malaria.

Pierre de Fermat was a French jurist, classical scholar, and one of the great mathematical minds of the seventeenth century. Working mostly outside academic institutions, he helped shape number theory, analytic geometry, probability, optics, and early ideas that later fed into calculus. His name is forever tied to Fermat’s Last Theorem, a marginal note that challenged mathematicians for centuries. He died in Castres on 12 January 1665, apparently after illness, and epitaph-based research indicates he was 57 years old.

Gamal Abdel Nasser was an Egyptian military officer and revolutionary leader who became one of the defining political figures of the modern Arab world. After helping lead the 1952 revolution that ended Egypt’s monarchy, he served as president, championed Arab nationalism, nationalized the Suez Canal, promoted major modernization projects such as the Aswan High Dam, and briefly led the United Arab Republic with Syria. He died in Cairo on 28 September 1970, aged 52, after suffering a heart attack shortly after the close of an Arab League summit, prompting massive public mourning across Egypt and the Arab world.

Famous for his six marriages, his break with Rome, and the establishment of royal supremacy over the Church of England, he reshaped English politics, religion, and monarchy. He died in Prague on 24 October 1601, aged 54, after an acute bladder or kidney illness that followed a banquet; later studies found no convincing evidence that mercury poisoning killed him.

David Livingstone was a Scottish physician, Congregationalist missionary, and African explorer whose travels made him one of the best-known Victorian figures. Ivan IV Vasilyevich, known as Ivan the Terrible, was Grand Prince of Moscow and the first Tsar of Russia, ruling during a dramatic transformation of Muscovy into a more centralized and expansionist state. His reign included legal and military reforms, the conquest of Kazan and Astrakhan, and the violent oprichnina that left a lasting mark on Russian history. He died in Moscow on 28 March 1584, traditionally said to have suffered a stroke while playing chess, leaving the throne to his son Feodor I.

Park Chung Hee was a South Korean army officer and politician who ruled South Korea from his 1961 military coup through his presidency from 1963 to 1979. His government drove rapid industrialization and the so-called Miracle on the Han River, while also suppressing dissent under an authoritarian system. He was assassinated in Seoul on 26 October 1979 by Kim Jae-gyu, the head of the Korean Central Intelligence Agency, during a private dinner near the Blue House.

He led the Luftwaffe, helped build the Nazi police state, and accumulated vast political influence and looted art during the regime. Edward Gibbon

Birth date: May 7, 1737

Death date: January 15, 1794

Age: 56

Edward Gibbon was a British historian, essayist and parliamentarian, best known for The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, a monumental six-volume work admired for its sharp prose, command of sources and Enlightenment skepticism. His history helped shape modern historical writing and remains one of the great classics of English literature. In his final months, Gibbon suffered severely from a hydrocele; after repeated surgical treatment, complications following a third operation proved fatal. He died in London on 16 January 1794, aged 56.

Henry IV of France

Birth date: December 12, 1553

Death date: May 13, 1610

Age: 56

Henry IV of France, also known as Henry of Navarre, was the first Bourbon king of France and one of the central figures in the French Wars of Religion. Raised Protestant and later converting to Catholicism to secure the French throne, he helped stabilize a divided kingdom and is closely associated with the Edict of Nantes and pragmatic religious compromise. He died in Paris on 14 May 1610, when François Ravaillac, a Catholic zealot, stabbed him while his royal coach was stopped in traffic.

Pierre-Joseph Proudhon

Birth date: January 14, 1809

Death date: January 18, 1865

Age: 56

Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was a French socialist, philosopher, economist, journalist, and political theorist best remembered as a founder of mutualism and one of the earliest major thinkers to call himself an anarchist. His famous phrase “property is theft” made him a defining voice in nineteenth-century debates over property, labor, federalism, and liberty. After exile, imprisonment, and years of intense work, his health declined; he died in Passy, Paris, on 19 January 1865, reportedly after a final illness and in the presence of his wife and a close friend.

Antonio Gramsci

Birth date: January 21, 1891

Death date: April 26, 1937

Age: 46

Antonio Gramsci was an Italian Marxist philosopher, journalist, linguist, and politician, best known as a co-founder and former leader of the Italian Communist Party and for developing the influential theory of cultural hegemony. His Prison Notebooks, written under Fascist imprisonment, became a landmark of twentieth-century political thought. Arrested by Mussolini’s regime in 1926, he spent years in harsh confinement as his health collapsed. Moved between prison hospitals and clinics, he died in Rome on 27 April 1937 after a cerebral hemorrhage, aged 46.

Federico García Lorca

Birth date: June 4, 1898

Death date: August 18, 1936

Age: 38

Federico García Lorca was a Spanish poet, playwright, and theatre director, celebrated as one of the defining voices of the Generation of ’27. His works, including Gypsy Ballads, Blood Wedding, Yerma, and The House of Bernarda Alba, fused Andalusian tradition, lyric intensity, and modernist experimentation. At the start of the Spanish Civil War, he was arrested and executed by Nationalist forces near Granada; his body was never recovered, making his death one of the enduring tragedies of modern Spanish culture.

Ian Fleming

Birth date: May 27, 1908

Death date: August 11, 1964

Age: 56

Ian Lancaster Fleming was a British writer, journalist and former naval intelligence officer best remembered for creating James Bond, Agent 007. Drawing on wartime intelligence work, travel and journalism, he wrote Casino Royale and the Bond novels that became a global literary and film phenomenon, as well as Chitty-Chitty-Bang-Bang. A heavy smoker and drinker who suffered from heart disease, Fleming collapsed after dinner in Canterbury and died at Kent and Canterbury Hospital on 12 August 1964, aged 56, following heart failure/another heart attack.

Gustav Klimt

Birth date: July 13, 1862

Death date: February 5, 1918

Age: 55

Gustav Klimt was an Austrian Symbolist painter and a founder of the Vienna Secession, celebrated for richly ornamental works such as The Kiss and Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I. His art helped shape European Art Nouveau, blending decorative pattern, sensual portraiture, allegory, and gold leaf into a style that remains instantly recognizable. In early 1918 he suffered a stroke and then developed pneumonia; he died in Vienna on 6 February 1918 at the age of 55.

Death date: April 14, 1765

Age: 53

Mikhail Vasilyevich Lomonosov was a Russian polymath whose work ranged across chemistry, physics, astronomy, geology, mineralogy, language, poetry, and education. He is remembered for major scientific and cultural contributions, including work linked to the atmosphere of Venus, conservation of mass, Russian literary language, and the founding of Moscow University. He died in Saint Petersburg on 15 April 1765 at the age of 53, after a demanding career of scholarship and public service.

Erwin Rommel

Birth date: November 14, 1891

Death date: October 13, 1944

Age: 52
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Erwin Rommel is highly controversial because he was a senior commander in Nazi Germany's armed forces during World War II. His image has been shaped by propaganda and postwar mythmaking, including claims about his professionalism and distance from Nazi crimes, while historians continue to debate his relationship to the regime and his responsibility as an Axis commander.

Erwin Rommel was a German field marshal of World War II, best known as the “Desert Fox” for his command of Axis forces in North Africa and for his reputation as a bold armored-warfare tactician. His public image has remained contested, shaped by wartime propaganda, postwar mythmaking, and debate over his relationship to the Nazi regime. In October 1944, after being implicated in the aftermath of the 20 July plot against Hitler, he was forced to choose between trial and suicide; he died by cyanide poisoning at age 52.

Abel Tasman

Birth date: December 31, 1603

Death date: October 9, 1659

Age: 56

Abel Janszoon Tasman was a Dutch seafarer, merchant, and VOC explorer whose 1642 and 1644 voyages reshaped European knowledge of the southern Pacific. He made the first recorded European sightings of Tasmania and New Zealand, and his name still survives in Tasmania and the Tasman Sea. After retiring in Batavia, he wrote a will in 1657 while ill but not bedridden; he died there on 10 October 1659, survived by his second wife and a daughter.

Death date: July 7, 1967

Age: 53

Vivien Leigh was a British actress celebrated for her intensity, elegance, and two Academy Award-winning performances: Scarlett O'Hara in Gone with the Wind and Blanche DuBois in A Streetcar Named Desire. Though world-famous on screen, she remained deeply committed to stage work, performing Shakespeare, Coward, and Shaw across a demanding career. She died in London on 8 July 1967 at age 53 after long struggles with recurrent tuberculosis, an illness that had affected her health for decades.

Frank Zappa

Birth date: December 20, 1940

Death date: December 3, 1993

Age: 52

Frank Vincent Zappa was an American composer, guitarist, songwriter, bandleader, filmmaker, satirist, and one of rock music’s great iconoclasts. Over a career of more than three decades, he fused rock, jazz, orchestral music, doo-wop, musique concrète, and biting social commentary into a fiercely original body of work, recording with the Mothers of Invention and as a solo artist. Known for his musical complexity, independence, humor, and attacks on censorship, he became a major influence on experimental and progressive musicians. Zappa died at his Los Angeles home on December 4, 1993, from prostate cancer, after an illness diagnosed too late to be operable. He was 52 years old.

Johann Gottlieb Fichte

Birth date: May 18, 1762

Death date: January 28, 1814

Age: 51

Johann Gottlieb Fichte was a German philosopher and one of the founding figures of German Idealism after Kant. He is known for his theory of self-consciousness, his Wissenschaftslehre, and his politically charged Addresses to the German Nation. During the anti-Napoleonic crisis in Berlin, his wife nursed sick soldiers and contracted a fever; after she began to recover, Fichte himself fell ill, commonly described as typhus or hospital fever, and died in Berlin at the age of 51.

Édouard Manet

Birth date: January 22, 1832

Death date: April 29, 1883

Age: 51

Édouard Manet was a French painter whose bold treatment of modern Parisian life helped push European art from Realism toward Impressionism and modernism. Works such as Le Déjeuner sur l’herbe, Olympia, and A Bar at the Folies-Bergère challenged academic taste and made him a central figure of the avant-garde. In his final years he suffered severe pain and partial paralysis, commonly linked to syphilis and rheumatism; gangrene led to the amputation of his left foot shortly before he died in Paris at 51.

Arthur Rimbaud was a French poet whose fierce, visionary writing helped reshape modern poetry before he abandoned literature in his early twenties. Associated with Symbolism and remembered for works such as A Season in Hell and Illuminations, he became a restless traveler and trader after his literary career. In 1891, after a painful knee tumor, his leg was amputated in Marseille; cancer continued to advance, and he died there on 10 November 1891 at the age of 37.

Swami Vivekananda

Birth date: January 11, 1863

Death date: July 3, 1902

Age: 39

Swami Vivekananda, born Narendranath Datta, was an Indian Hindu monk, philosopher, author, and the leading disciple of Ramakrishna. He became one of the most influential modern interpreters of Vedanta and Yoga, gaining international fame after his 1893 address at the World’s Parliament of Religions in Chicago. He founded the Ramakrishna Mission and helped shape modern Hindu thought and Indian nationalism. After years of intense travel, teaching, and declining health, he died quietly at Belur Math on 4 July 1902, reportedly while meditating; a cerebral blood vessel rupture has been suggested as a possible cause.

Mikhail Bulgakov

Birth date: May 14, 1891

Death date: March 9, 1940

Age: 48

Mikhail Bulgakov was a Russian and Soviet novelist, playwright, and former physician whose sharp satire and fantastical imagination made him one of the defining literary figures of the 20th century. He is best remembered for The Master and Margarita, published after his death, as well as The White Guard and The Days of the Turbins. Frequently censored and politically pressured, he struggled for recognition during his lifetime. In his final years he suffered from severe kidney disease, commonly described as nephrosclerosis or nephrotic syndrome, and died in Moscow on 10 March 1940 at the age of 48.

James Fenimore Cooper

Birth date: September 14, 1789

Death date: September 13, 1851

Age: 61

James Fenimore Cooper was a pioneering American novelist whose frontier romances, especially The Last of the Mohicans and the Leatherstocking Tales, helped define early U.S. historical fiction and the literary image of the American wilderness. A former U.S. Navy midshipman, he also wrote influential sea stories. He spent his later years in Cooperstown, New York, and died there on September 14, 1851, one day before his 62nd birthday; older accounts describe his final illness as dropsy.

Théophile Gautier

Birth date: August 29, 1811

Death date: October 22, 1872

Age: 61

Théophile Gautier was a French poet, novelist, dramatist, journalist, and art critic, remembered as a brilliant defender of Romanticism and a writer whose cult of beauty helped shape later Parnassian, Symbolist, Decadent, and Modernist traditions. He wrote works such as Mademoiselle de Maupin, Émaux et camées, and Le Capitaine Fracasse, and was admired by figures including Baudelaire, Flaubert, Proust, and Wilde. In his last years he lived through the Franco-Prussian War and the Paris Commune in Paris; weakened by long-standing cardiac disease, he died at Neuilly-sur-Seine on 23 October 1872, aged 61, and was buried in Montmartre Cemetery.

Death date: May 11, 1884

Age: 60

Bedřich Smetana was a Czech Romantic composer whose operas and symphonic poems helped define a national musical voice for Bohemia. He is best known for The Bartered Bride and Má vlast, including the famous tone poem Vltava, or The Moldau. By the end of 1874 he was completely deaf, yet he continued composing some of his most enduring music. In his final years he suffered depression, hallucinations, and severe mental decline, probably linked to syphilis; his family placed him in a Prague asylum shortly before his death there at age 60.

Ramakrishna

Birth date: February 17, 1836

Death date: August 15, 1886

Age: 50

Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, born Gadadhar Chattopadhyay, was a 19th-century Indian Hindu mystic and priest whose teachings emphasized direct spiritual experience and the unity of religious paths. Associated with the Dakshineswar Kali Temple, he drew disciples including Swami Vivekananda, who later spread his message widely. In his final year he suffered from throat cancer and was cared for by disciples at Cossipore, where he died on 16 August 1886 at age 50.

Malcolm X

Death date: February 20, 1965

Age: 39

Malcolm X, born Malcolm Little and later known as el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz, was an influential African American minister, public speaker, and Black nationalist leader. He rose to prominence as a major voice of the Nation of Islam before breaking with the organization in 1964 and founding Muslim Mosque, Inc. and the Organization of Afro-American Unity. A forceful advocate for Black dignity, self-determination, and human rights, he remains one of the most important figures of the civil rights era. He was assassinated by gunfire on February 21, 1965, while preparing to speak at the Audubon Ballroom in New York City, dying at age 39.

Otto I the Great

Birth date: November 22, 912

Death date: May 6, 973

Age: 60

Otto I, known as Otto the Great, was duke of Saxony, king of East Francia/Germany, king of Italy, and Holy Roman Emperor from 962. He strengthened royal authority, relied heavily on bishops and abbots as imperial administrators, subdued rebellious nobles, and won lasting fame by defeating the Magyars at Lechfeld in 955. In his final year he returned from Italy to Germany after securing the succession of his son Otto II. During Rogation Days at Memleben, the palace where his father had died, he fell seriously ill with fever, received the last sacraments, and died on 7 May 973 at the age of 60.

Birth date: January 21, 1729

Death date: February 14, 1781

Age: 52

Gotthold Ephraim Lessing was a central figure of the German Enlightenment: a playwright, philosopher, critic, publicist, and early dramaturg whose works such as “Emilia Galotti,” “Nathan the Wise,” and “Laocoön” helped reshape German literature and theatre. His writing argued for intellectual freedom, religious tolerance, and a more independent German dramatic tradition. In his final years his health worsened; after asthma attacks, a winter cold, and a collapse in Braunschweig, he died there on 15 February 1781, reportedly after treatment for chest dropsy, at the age of 52.

Death date: March 30, 1855

Age: 38

Charlotte Brontë was an English novelist and poet, one of the celebrated Brontë siblings, and the author of Jane Eyre, published in 1847 under the pseudonym Currer Bell. Her work brought emotional intensity, social criticism, and psychological depth to Victorian fiction. She married Arthur Bell Nicholls in 1854 and died in Haworth on 31 March 1855, while pregnant, shortly before her 39th birthday. Her death certificate recorded phthisis, though later scholars have suggested complications of severe pregnancy sickness may also have played a role.

Death date: December 20, 1940

Age: 44

F. Scott Fitzgerald was an American novelist, essayist, and short story writer whose work helped define the Jazz Age, a term he helped popularize. He is best remembered for The Great Gatsby, as well as This Side of Paradise, The Beautiful and Damned, and Tender Is the Night. His sharp portraits of ambition, wealth, romance, and disillusion made him one of the major American writers of the 20th century. After years of financial strain, declining health, and work as a Hollywood screenwriter, he died of a heart attack in Los Angeles on December 21, 1940, at age 44.

Carl von Clausewitz was a Prussian army officer, major general, and military theorist whose unfinished work On War became one of the most influential texts on strategy, politics, and the nature of conflict. In 1831, while serving in Breslau during efforts connected to the cholera crisis, he contracted the disease and died after a short illness at the age of 51.

Isabella I of Castile, known as Isabella the Catholic, was queen of Castile and León and, through her marriage to Ferdinand II, a central figure in the dynastic union that shaped early modern Spain. Her reign saw the completion of the Reconquista, the sponsorship of Christopher Columbus’s 1492 voyage, and the rise of Spain as a major European and overseas power. She died at Medina del Campo on 26 November 1504, after a period of declining health often associated with uterine cancer and fluid retention, at the age of 53.

Death date: December 28, 1986

Age: 54

Andrei Tarkovsky was a Soviet film director, screenwriter, and theorist whose meditative style, long takes, spiritual themes, and dreamlike imagery made him one of cinema’s most influential artists. His major films include Ivan's Childhood, Andrei Rublev, Solaris, Mirror, Stalker, Nostalghia, and The Sacrifice. After conflicts with Soviet film authorities, he worked abroad in his final years. He died in France on 29 December 1986 at age 54 after suffering from cancer, commonly reported as lung cancer, leaving behind a compact but profoundly influential body of work.

Age: 54

Husayn ibn Ali was a central religious and political figure of early Islam: the son of Ali and Fatima, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, younger brother of Hasan ibn Ali, and revered in Shia Islam as the third Imam. His refusal to recognize the authority of the Umayyad caliph Yazid I led to his stand at Karbala, where he and many of his small group of relatives and supporters were killed in 680. His death became one of the defining martyrdoms of Islamic history and remains commemorated during Ashura.

Death date: October 15, 1793

Age: 37

Marie Antoinette was an Austrian archduchess who became Queen of France as the wife of Louis XVI. A highly visible figure at Versailles, she became associated with court luxury, political distrust, and the mounting tensions that preceded the French Revolution. After the monarchy was overthrown, she was imprisoned, tried by the Revolutionary Tribunal, convicted of high treason, and executed by guillotine in Paris on 16 October 1793.

Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Heinrich Himmler was one of the central leaders of Nazi Germany and a principal architect of the Holocaust. As Reichsfuhrer-SS, he oversaw the SS, concentration and extermination camp systems, mass murder, racial persecution, police terror, and other crimes against humanity.

Heinrich Himmler was a German Nazi politician and military leader, best known as Reichsführer-SS and one of the most powerful figures in Nazi Germany. He built the SS into a vast instrument of terror, controlled major police and security forces, and played a central role in organizing the Holocaust and Nazi occupation policies. In the final weeks of World War II, after failed attempts to negotiate with the Western Allies, he was dismissed by Hitler, captured by British forces, and died by suicide in custody on 23 May 1945 at the age of 44.

Why this is controversial: Maximilien Robespierre is highly controversial because he is closely associated with the Reign of Terror during the French Revolution, political repression, revolutionary tribunals, and mass executions by guillotine. His defenders point to his democratic, anti-slavery, and egalitarian positions, but his name remains strongly linked to state violence and ideological extremism.

Maximilien Robespierre was a French lawyer, Jacobin politician, and one of the most influential figures of the French Revolution. He championed political equality, universal male suffrage, civic virtue, and the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade, while becoming closely associated with the Committee of Public Safety and the Reign of Terror. In July 1794, amid rising fear of his power and policies, he was overthrown in the Thermidorian Reaction, arrested, and guillotined in Paris without trial at the age of 36.

Nero was the fifth Roman emperor and the last ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, reigning from AD 54 to 68. Remembered for his theatrical tastes, ambitious building projects, political violence, and the controversies surrounding the Great Fire of Rome, he remains one of antiquity’s most notorious rulers. Facing rebellion, abandonment by key supporters, and condemnation by the Senate, Nero fled Rome and died by suicide on 9 June AD 68 at the age of 30.

Nelson died at age 47 during the Battle of Trafalgar on 21 October 1805, after being struck by enemy fire aboard HMS Victory; the battle was a decisive British triumph.

Walter Benjamin was a German-Jewish philosopher, cultural critic, essayist, and media theorist whose writings on art, literature, history, technology, and modern urban life became central to twentieth-century critical theory. In January 41 he was assassinated at the Palatine Games in a conspiracy led by Praetorian officers, ending his reign at age 28.

Alexander III of Russia was Emperor of Russia, King of Poland, and Grand Duke of Finland from 1881 until 1894. A firm autocrat, he reversed many of Alexander II’s liberal reforms, promoted Russian nationalism, and became known as “the Peacemaker” because Russia fought no major wars during his reign. His later years were marked by declining health, and in 1894 he became gravely ill with kidney disease. Too weak to travel farther, he remained at Livadia in Crimea, where he died on 1 November 1894 at the age of 49.

Alfred de Musset

Birth date: December 10, 1810

Death date: May 1, 1857

Age: 46

Alfred de Musset was a leading French Romantic poet, dramatist, and novelist, remembered for works such as Lorenzaccio, On ne badine pas avec l’amour, and the autobiographical novel La Confession d’un enfant du siècle. A brilliant, emotionally intense figure of 19th-century literature, he became associated with youthful passion, irony, disillusionment, and the artistic circles of Paris. He died in Paris in his sleep on 2 May 1857, aged 46; accounts commonly connect his final illness with heart failure, long-standing aortic insufficiency, and the effects of alcoholism.

Zulfikar Ali Bhutto

Birth date: January 4, 1928

Death date: April 3, 1979

Age: 51
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Zulfikar Ali Bhutto is highly controversial because he was both a major democratic and constitutional figure and a polarizing ruler accused by critics of authoritarian tactics, political repression, and manipulation of state power. His murder conviction and execution remain deeply disputed, especially because Pakistan's Supreme Court later said his trial did not meet fair-trial standards.

Zulfikar Ali Bhutto was a Pakistani barrister, statesman, founder of the Pakistan People’s Party, and one of the country’s most influential political leaders. He served as president from 1971 to 1973 and prime minister from 1973 to 1977, playing a central role in Pakistan’s post-1971 reconstruction and the 1973 constitution. After being overthrown in a military coup, he was convicted in a controversial murder case and hanged in Rawalpindi on 4 April 1979; Pakistan’s Supreme Court later stated that his trial had not met fair-trial standards.

Margaret Mitchell

Birth date: November 7, 1900

Death date: August 15, 1949

Age: 48

Margaret Munnerlyn Mitchell was an American novelist and journalist from Atlanta, best known for writing Gone with the Wind, her only novel published during her lifetime. The book became a landmark of popular historical fiction and won major literary honors, including the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. On August 11, 1949, Mitchell was struck by a speeding car while crossing Peachtree Street in Atlanta with her husband on the way to a movie. She suffered severe injuries and died five days later, on August 16, at age 48.

Rosalind Franklin

Birth date: July 24, 1920

Death date: April 15, 1958

Age: 37

Rosalind Franklin was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer whose precise experimental work helped reveal the molecular structures of DNA, RNA, viruses, coal, and graphite. Her DNA research at King’s College London, especially the evidence connected with Photo 51, became central to the discovery of the double helix. She died in London of ovarian cancer on 16 April 1958, aged 37, before the Nobel Prize recognition given to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins in 1962.

Mikhail Yuryevich Lermontov was a major Russian Romantic poet, novelist, playwright, painter, and army officer whose works, especially A Hero of Our Time and his lyric poetry, helped shape modern Russian literature. Exiled to the Caucasus after the poem Death of the Poet made him famous, he later died in 1841 at age 26 after being shot in a duel with fellow officer Nikolai Martynov.

Xerxes I

Birth date: December 31, 519 BCE

Death date: August 5, 466 BCE

Age: 53

Xerxes I, also known as Xerxes the Great, was the fourth King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire and ruled Persia from 486 to 465 BCE. Son of Darius I and Atossa, he inherited a vast empire and is best remembered for the massive invasion of Greece in 480 BCE, including Thermopylae, Salamis, and the occupation of Athens. After returning to Persia, he invested heavily in royal construction at Persepolis and Susa. In 465 BCE, probably in August, he was assassinated in a palace conspiracy led by Artabanus, commander of the royal bodyguard, and was succeeded by Artaxerxes I.

Death date: October 20, 1969

Age: 47

Jack Kerouac was an American novelist and poet, best known as a central voice of the Beat Generation and the author of On the Road, whose restless prose helped shape postwar counterculture. Born in Lowell, Massachusetts to a French-Canadian family, he wrote about travel, spirituality, friendship, jazz, and the search for freedom. Kerouac died in St. Petersburg, Florida on October 21, 1969, at age 47, after internal hemorrhaging associated with cirrhosis and years of heavy drinking.

Why this is controversial: Cecil Rhodes is deeply controversial because of his role in British imperial expansion in southern Africa, the growth of De Beers, land dispossession, racial hierarchy, and policies connected to white settler rule. Cecil John Rhodes was a British mining magnate, politician, and imperial figure in southern Africa, best known for founding De Beers, serving as Prime Minister of the Cape Colony, and endowing the Rhodes Scholarship. His legacy remains deeply contested because of his role in colonial expansion and racially discriminatory policies. After years of poor health and heart problems, he died of heart failure at Muizenberg in the Cape Colony on 26 March 1902, aged 48.

Patrice Émery Lumumba was a Congolese nationalist, pan-Africanist, and the first prime minister of the independent Republic of the Congo in 1960. A powerful symbol of anti-colonial politics, he helped lead the country out of Belgian rule during one of Africa’s most turbulent independence moments. After being forced from office during the Congo Crisis, he was captured, transferred to Katanga, tortured, and executed by firing squad on 17 January 1961.

Basil of Caesarea, known as Saint Basil the Great, was a fourth-century Christian bishop, theologian, defender of the Nicene Creed, and one of the Cappadocian Fathers. Bishop of Caesarea from 370, he shaped Eastern Christian monastic life, argued against Arianism, and became famous for charitable institutions serving the poor and sick. He died in Caesarea on 1 January 379, probably around age 50; ancient accounts and modern summaries connect his early death with illness, especially liver disease, and with the strain of severe ascetic practices.
