Age: 50

Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, was a Piedmontese statesman, reformer, journalist, and one of the chief architects of Italian unification. As prime minister of the Kingdom of Sardinia and then the first prime minister of the Kingdom of Italy, he used diplomacy, economic modernization, and calculated alliances to turn Piedmont into the political engine of the Risorgimento. He died in Turin on 6 June 1861, only a few months after Italy was proclaimed a kingdom, following a sudden severe fever commonly attributed to malaria; he was 50.

Death date: July 31, 1714

Age: 49

Anne, Queen of Great Britain and Ireland, was the last Stuart monarch and the ruler under whom England and Scotland were united by the Acts of Union in 1707. Her reign was marked by the War of the Spanish Succession, fierce Whig-Tory rivalries, and the growing power of ministers. Chronically ill for much of her life and devastated by the deaths of all her children, she became unable to walk in her final years, suffered a stroke on 30 July 1714, and died at Kensington Palace on 1 August 1714, aged 49.

George Boole was an English self-taught mathematician, philosopher, and logician whose work transformed symbolic logic and laid foundations for Boolean algebra, a cornerstone of modern computing and digital circuit design. He became the first professor of mathematics at Queen's College, Cork, and wrote the influential The Laws of Thought. In late 1864, after walking to lecture through heavy rain and remaining in wet clothes, he developed pneumonia and died in Cork from related complications at the age of 49.

Age: 48

Anna Politkovskaya was a Russian investigative journalist and writer best known for her courageous reporting on the Second Chechen War, human rights abuses, corruption, and the abuses of power under Vladimir Putin. Writing for Novaya Gazeta, she became one of Russia’s most internationally recognized voices for victims of war and state violence. After years of threats, intimidation, detention, and an alleged poisoning attempt, she was shot dead in the elevator of her Moscow apartment building on 7 October 2006. Several men were later convicted for the murder, but the person or people who ordered it have never been definitively identified.

Gaius Valerius Catullus was one of the sharpest and most personal poets of the late Roman Republic, famous for intense love poems, polished insults, and the emotionally charged figure of Lesbia. He died young in Rome around 54 BCE, probably at about 30; no reliable ancient account records the medical cause or precise circumstances of his death.

Abbas the Great, or Shah Abbas I, was the fifth Safavid shah of Iran and one of the most celebrated rulers in Iranian history. He strengthened the Safavid state, reorganized the army, fought the Ottomans and Uzbeks, moved the capital to Isfahan, and promoted commerce, architecture, and the arts. His final years were shadowed by poor health and succession anxieties; he died in Mazandaran, at or near Farahabad on the Caspian coast, in January 1629 at age 57 and was buried in Kashan.

Death date: March 23, 1455

Age: 57

Pope Nicholas V, born Tommaso Parentucelli in Sarzana, was head of the Catholic Church from 1447 to 1455 and one of the key patrons of the early Roman Renaissance. He promoted humanist scholarship, strengthened Rome, restored churches and aqueducts, and laid plans connected with the future rebuilding of St. Peter’s Basilica. His pontificate also faced the shock of Constantinople’s fall in 1453, after which he called for a crusade that never truly materialized. He died in Rome on 24 March 1455 at the age of 57.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Joseph Smith is a deeply contested religious and political founder. Controversies include the origins and truth claims of the Book of Mormon, plural marriage, theocratic power in Nauvoo, conflict with critics, destruction of an opposition press, and the enduring divide between believers' and critics' accounts of his life.

Joseph Smith Jr. was an American religious and political leader best known as the founder of Mormonism and the Latter Day Saint movement. He published the Book of Mormon in 1830 and organized a church that later developed into several denominations, including the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. His teachings, revelations, and leadership attracted many followers but also intense opposition. In 1844, after conflict in Nauvoo, Illinois, Smith was jailed in Carthage and was shot and killed by a mob at the age of 38.

Why this is controversial: John, King of England, has a long-standing reputation for arbitrary rule, heavy taxation, military failure, conflict with the church and barons, and harsh treatment of rivals and prisoners. His reign led directly to the Magna Carta crisis, and he remains one of the more negatively remembered English monarchs.

John, King of England from 1199 to 1216, was the youngest son of Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine and is remembered as John Lackland. His reign saw the loss of Normandy to Philip II of France, conflict with the papacy, heavy taxation, and the baronial crisis that led to the sealing of Magna Carta in 1215. During the First Barons' War, while campaigning in eastern England, he became seriously ill, probably with dysentery, and died at Newark Castle on 19 October 1216.

Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, born Ibrahim Awwad Ibrahim Ali al-Badri, was an Iraqi militant leader who rose from the post-2003 insurgency to become the first leader of the Islamic State. Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Mary I of England is highly controversial because her attempt to restore Roman Catholicism included the Marian persecutions, in which hundreds of Protestants were burned for heresy. Her reign is remembered through the hostile nickname “Bloody Mary,” and debates around religious violence, dynastic power, and repression remain central to her reputation.

Mary I, often called Mary Tudor, was Queen of England and Ireland from 1553 to 1558 and the first queen regnant of England. The daughter of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon, she tried to restore Roman Catholicism after the English Reformation and became notorious for the Marian persecutions of Protestants. Her marriage to Philip of Spain was politically divisive, and she left no child. She grew weak and ill in 1558, possibly from ovarian cysts or uterine cancer, and died at St James's Palace during an influenza epidemic at the age of 42.

Guillaume Apollinaire was a Polish-French poet, playwright, novelist, journalist, and art critic who helped shape the avant-garde culture of early twentieth-century Paris. A passionate defender of Cubism and an important precursor of Surrealism, he wrote influential works such as Alcools and Calligrammes and helped modern poetry break away from older forms. During World War I he served in the French army and suffered a serious head wound in 1916. Weakened by that injury, he died in Paris during the 1918 influenza pandemic, just two days before the Armistice, at the age of 38.

Titus Flavius Vespasianus was Roman emperor from 79 to 81 CE and a leading figure of the Flavian dynasty. Before ruling, he commanded Roman forces in the Jewish War and captured Jerusalem in 70, an event later commemorated by the Arch of Titus. As emperor he completed the Colosseum and became known for disaster relief after Vesuvius and a major fire in Rome. His reign was brief: after the amphitheatre games, he fell ill and died of fever on 13 September 81, aged 41, and was succeeded by his brother Domitian.

Domitian, born Titus Flavius Domitianus, was Roman emperor from 81 to 96 CE and the last ruler of the Flavian dynasty. The son of Vespasian and younger brother of Titus, he strengthened imperial administration, promoted major building projects, and maintained strong support among the army and people, while alienating much of the Senate through authoritarian rule. Srinivasa Ramanujan

Birth date: December 21, 1887

Death date: April 25, 1920

Age: 32

Srinivasa Ramanujan was an Indian mathematician whose extraordinary intuition transformed number theory, infinite series, continued fractions, partitions, and modular forms. Largely self-taught, he developed thousands of identities and formulas, many later proved correct and influential. His correspondence with G. H. Hardy brought him to Cambridge, where his originality astonished leading mathematicians. In 1919, worsening illness forced him to return to India; he died in Kumbakonam on 26 April 1920, aged 32, while still producing new mathematical ideas.

Max Stirner

Birth date: October 24, 1806

Death date: June 25, 1856

Age: 49

Max Stirner, born Johann Caspar Schmidt, was a German philosopher associated with the Young Hegelians and best known for The Ego and Its Own, a radical defense of individual self-ownership that later influenced egoism, individualist anarchism, and critiques of ideology. He spent much of his life as a teacher, writer, and translator in Berlin, often in financial difficulty. In 1856, still obscure and poor, he developed a severe fever or tumor reportedly following an insect bite or sting on the neck. He died in Berlin at age 49, with only a small circle aware of his passing.

Selim I

Birth date: October 9, 1470

Death date: September 21, 1520

Age: 49
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Selim I is highly controversial because his reign involved aggressive imperial expansion, major wars against the Safavids and Mamluks, dynastic executions, and severe violence against groups seen as internal enemies, especially Qizilbash and Alevi-associated communities. His nickname, Selim the Grim, reflects a reputation for severity and brutality.

Selim I, known as Yavuz Sultan Selim or Selim the Grim, was the Ottoman sultan from 1512 to 1520. In only eight years he dramatically expanded Ottoman power, defeating the Safavids at Chaldiran and conquering the Mamluk Sultanate, bringing Syria, Egypt, the Hejaz, and key pilgrimage routes under Ottoman control. He died near Çorlu after a severe illness, traditionally linked to a badly treated carbuncle or boil, though later writers have suggested other causes such as cancer or plague.

Charles the Bald, also known as Charles II, was a Carolingian ruler, the youngest son of Louis the Pious and a grandson of Charlemagne. His reign was shaped by dynastic conflict, Viking pressure, and the fragile rebuilding of imperial authority. He died in 877 at about 54 while returning from Italy, after falling ill during a campaign to defend his imperial claims.

Death date: December 19, 69

Age: 54

Aulus Vitellius was a Roman aristocrat and military commander who became emperor in AD 69, the turbulent Year of the Four Emperors. Backed by the Rhine legions after Galba’s fall and Otho’s defeat, he ruled for only about eight months and was remembered for indulgence, factional violence, and poor discipline among his supporters. When Vespasian’s forces advanced on Rome, Vitellius tried to abdicate but was prevented by his own party. After brutal fighting in the city, he was captured, dragged through Rome, killed at the Gemonian stairs, and his body was thrown into the Tiber.

He died in Uppsala from tuberculosis in 1744, only 42 years old, before the Celsius scale was reversed into its modern form.

Shaka kaSenzangakhona, widely known as Shaka Zulu, was the powerful founder and king of the Zulu Kingdom, remembered for reshaping military organization, discipline, and regional politics in southern Africa. His reign from about 1816 to 1828 helped turn the Zulu from a smaller chiefdom into a major force. He was assassinated at KwaDukuza by his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana, with Mbopa also traditionally named among the conspirators, after mounting tensions in the royal court.

Sylvia Plath was an American poet, novelist, and short-story writer whose intense, sharply crafted work helped define confessional poetry. Alfred Lothar Wegener was a German meteorologist, geophysicist, polar researcher, and the scientist who proposed the continental drift hypothesis, a once-ridiculed idea that later became central to plate tectonics. After leaving with Rasmus Villumsen for the west coast, Wegener died on the ice, probably from exhaustion and heart failure; his body was found months later.

Why this is controversial: Jean-Paul Marat is highly controversial because of his radical journalism during the French Revolution, his calls for harsh action against perceived enemies of the revolution, and his association with the political atmosphere that led to revolutionary violence and the Reign of Terror. His murder also turned him into a polarizing revolutionary martyr.

Jean-Paul Marat was a French revolutionary journalist, physician, scientist, and political theorist whose newspaper L'Ami du peuple made him one of the most uncompromising voices of the radical movement during the French Revolution. A fierce defender of the sans-culottes and a figure associated with the Montagnards, he became both influential and deeply divisive. Suffering from a severe skin condition, he often worked from a medicinal bath; on 13 July 1793, he was stabbed there by Charlotte Corday, a Girondin sympathizer, and soon became a revolutionary martyr.

Lavrentiy Pavlovich Beria was a Georgian-born Soviet politician and one of Joseph Stalin’s most powerful security chiefs, leading the NKVD and later holding senior posts in the Soviet government. He was deeply involved in Stalinist repression, wartime internal security, deportations, and the Soviet atomic project. After Stalin’s death, Beria briefly seemed positioned for even greater power, but was arrested during a leadership struggle, tried for treason and other crimes, and executed by shooting in Moscow on 23 December 1953.

TutanKhamun

Birth date: December 31, 1343 BCE

Death date: December 31, 1324 BCE

Age: 19

Tutankhamun, often called King Tut, was a pharaoh of Egypt's Eighteenth Dynasty who came to the throne as a child and helped restore the traditional religion after the Amarna period. His own reign was brief, but his fame became global after Howard Carter discovered his remarkably rich tomb in 1922. He died young at about 19, probably after a combination of illness and physical injury, and his unexpected death helps explain why he was buried in a relatively small tomb that still transformed modern understanding of ancient Egypt.

James Dean

Birth date: February 7, 1931

Death date: September 29, 1955

Age: 24

James Dean was an American actor whose intense performances in East of Eden, Rebel Without a Cause, and Giant made him one of the defining screen icons of the 1950s. His career was remarkably short, but his brooding style and rebellious image left a lasting mark on film and popular culture; he died in a car crash near Cholame, California, on September 30, 1955, at the age of 24.

Lesya Ukrainka

Birth date: February 24, 1871

Death date: July 31, 1913

Age: 42

Lesya Ukrainka, born Larysa Petrivna Kosach, was one of Ukraine’s great literary voices: a poet, playwright, translator, intellectual, and activist whose works such as Forest Song helped shape modern Ukrainian literature. A lifelong illness forced her to travel widely in search of treatment, but it did not quiet her public spirit or creative discipline. She died in Surami, Georgia, after a long struggle with tuberculosis affecting her bones, lungs, and kidneys, with family caring for her in her final days.

Francis Xavier

Birth date: April 6, 1506

Death date: December 2, 1552

Age: 46

Francis Xavier was a Navarrese Catholic cleric, missionary, and co-founder of the Society of Jesus. A close companion of Ignatius of Loyola, he became one of the most influential Christian missionaries of the early modern era, working across India, Southeast Asia, and Japan and helping launch the first major Christian mission to Japan. In 1552 he tried to enter Ming China but was stranded on Shangchuan Island, where he fell ill while waiting for passage to the mainland. He died there on 3 December 1552 at the age of 46.

Joseph Addison

Birth date: April 30, 1672

Death date: June 16, 1719

Age: 47

Joseph Addison was an influential English essayist, poet, playwright, and Whig politician, best remembered for his partnership with Richard Steele and for shaping the elegant, conversational style of The Tatler and The Spectator. His tragedy Cato also became one of the best-known English plays of the early eighteenth century. In later life his health declined badly; he resigned high office in 1718 and died at Holland House, London, on 17 June 1719, reportedly after asthma was complicated by dropsy.

Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec

Birth date: November 23, 1864

Death date: September 8, 1901

Age: 36

Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec was a French painter, printmaker, draughtsman, caricaturist, and illustrator whose sharp, vivid scenes of Parisian nightlife made him one of the defining artists of fin-de-siècle Montmartre. Born into an aristocratic family, he became closely associated with cabarets, performers, cafés, and brothels, creating iconic images of the Moulin Rouge and the bohemian world around it. His health declined severely in his final years, worsened by alcoholism and syphilis; after strokes and paralysis, he died at his mother's estate, Château Malromé, on 9 September 1901, aged 36.

Gustav Stresemann

Birth date: May 9, 1878

Death date: October 2, 1929

Age: 51

Gustav Stresemann was a German statesman of the Weimar Republic, briefly chancellor in 1923 and foreign minister from 1923 to 1929. He helped stabilize Germany after hyperinflation, pursued reconciliation with France, supported the Locarno Treaties, and shared the 1926 Nobel Peace Prize with Aristide Briand. In his final years his health deteriorated under intense political strain, and he died in Berlin after strokes on 3 October 1929, aged 51.

Paul II

Birth date: February 22, 1417

Death date: July 25, 1471

Age: 54

Pope Paul II, born Pietro Barbo in Venice, led the Catholic Church and ruled the Papal States from 1464 to 1471. A nephew of Pope Eugene IV, he rose quickly through the Church, became a cardinal while still young, and was remembered for his wealth, taste for ceremony, and interest in art, antiquities, and the rebuilding of Rome. He died suddenly in Rome on 26 July 1471 at age 54, commonly described as a heart attack, though contemporary and later accounts gave differing explanations for the suddenness of his death.

Billie Holiday

Birth date: April 6, 1915

Death date: July 16, 1959

Age: 44

Billie Holiday, born Eleanora Fagan and nicknamed “Lady Day,” was one of the most influential American jazz and swing singers of the twentieth century. Her phrasing, emotional timing, and unmistakable voice changed the way popular songs could be sung, and recordings such as “Strange Fruit,” “God Bless the Child,” and “Lady Sings the Blues” helped define her legacy. Her later years were marked by legal troubles, addiction, and declining health. She died in New York City on July 17, 1959, at age 44, after severe illness linked to cirrhosis and heart failure.

Thomas Sankara

Birth date: December 20, 1949

Death date: October 14, 1987

Age: 37

Thomas Sankara was a Burkinabé military officer, Pan-Africanist revolutionary, and president of Burkina Faso from 1983 to 1987. He became known for anti-corruption measures, mass vaccination drives, literacy efforts, reforestation, women’s rights reforms, and renaming Upper Volta as Burkina Faso. His bold socialist and anti-imperialist agenda made him an enduring symbol of African self-reliance. On 15 October 1987, he was assassinated in Ouagadougou during a coup linked to his former ally Blaise Compaoré.

Anna Pavlova

Birth date: February 11, 1881

Death date: January 22, 1931

Age: 49

Anna Pavlova was a Russian prima ballerina whose delicate style and dramatic presence made her one of the most famous dancers of the early twentieth century. A star of the Imperial Russian Ballet and briefly associated with the Ballets Russes, she became inseparable from The Dying Swan and helped turn ballet into a global touring art. She died in The Hague on 23 January 1931, aged 49, after falling seriously ill while travelling; accounts commonly describe pleurisy, sometimes linked with pneumonia.

Bayezid I

Birth date: March 7, 1354

Death date: March 7, 1403

Age: 49

Bayezid I, known as Yıldırım or “the Thunderbolt,” was the fourth sultan of the Ottoman Empire, ruling from 1389 to 1402. A bold and fast-moving commander, he expanded Ottoman authority across Anatolia and the Balkans and defeated a major crusading army at Nicopolis in 1396. His rise was halted by Timur, who defeated and captured him at the Battle of Ankara in 1402. Bayezid died in captivity at Akşehir on 8 March 1403, and his death helped trigger the Ottoman Interregnum among his sons.

Sofia Kovalevskaya

Birth date: January 14, 1850

Death date: February 9, 1891

Age: 41

Sofya Kovalevskaya was a Russian mathematician and writer whose work in analysis, partial differential equations, and mechanics made her one of the most important scientists of the nineteenth century. She became the first woman in modern Europe to receive a doctorate in mathematics and later held a professorship in Stockholm, breaking barriers in a field that had almost entirely excluded women. She died in Stockholm on 10 February 1891, aged 41, after influenza developed into pneumonia following a trip to Nice.

Catherine of Aragon

Birth date: December 15, 1485

Death date: January 6, 1536

Age: 50

Catherine of Aragon was a Spanish princess, daughter of Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, and became Queen of England as the first wife of Henry VIII. Educated, politically capable, and widely respected, she served as regent in 1513 while Henry was in France and remained a symbol of dignity during the crisis over their marriage. After Henry sought an annulment and broke with papal authority, Catherine was removed from court and recognized only as Dowager Princess of Wales. She spent her final years at Kimbolton Castle, where she died on 7 January 1536, probably from cancer, at the age of 50.

Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit

Birth date: May 23, 1686

Death date: September 15, 1736

Age: 50

Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit was a physicist, inventor, and maker of scientific instruments, born in Gdańsk and active for much of his career in the Dutch Republic. He transformed temperature measurement by producing reliable thermometers, developing the mercury-in-glass thermometer, and creating the Fahrenheit scale. In early September 1736 he became seriously ill in The Hague, made and amended his will, and died there on 16 September 1736 at the age of 50. He was buried in the Kloosterkerk a few days later.

Louis Braille

Birth date: January 3, 1809

Death date: January 5, 1852

Age: 43

Louis Braille was a French educator, musician, and inventor whose six-dot tactile writing system transformed literacy for blind and visually impaired people around the world. Blinded in childhood after an accident in his father’s workshop, he became a gifted student at the Royal Institute for Blind Youth and developed braille while still a teenager. He later taught at the Institute and refined his system for reading, writing, and music. Braille suffered for many years from a serious respiratory illness, widely described as tuberculosis, and died in Paris on 1852-01-06, just two days after turning 43.

Christopher Marlowe

Birth date: February 25, 1564

Death date: May 29, 1593

Age: 29

Christopher Marlowe, also known as Kit Marlowe, was one of the defining voices of Elizabethan drama: a playwright, poet, translator, and major predecessor of Shakespeare. His bold blank verse and ambitious protagonists shaped the English stage through works such as Tamburlaine, Doctor Faustus, The Jew of Malta, and Edward II. His life ended abruptly in Deptford in 1593, when he was stabbed during a disputed altercation involving Ingram Frizer; the official account called it self-defence, though the circumstances have remained famously controversial.

Louis XII of France

Birth date: June 26, 1462

Death date: December 31, 1515

Age: 52

Louis XII of France, born Louis of Orléans, ruled France from 1498 to 1515 and was also briefly King of Naples. Remembered as the “Father of the People” for tax reductions, legal reforms, and relative domestic calm, he also pursued costly Italian campaigns and strengthened the link between Brittany and France through his marriage to Anne of Brittany. In his final months he married Mary Tudor in a last attempt to secure a male heir, but he was already in declining health. After a severe attack of gout around Christmas 1514, he received the final sacraments on 1 January 1515 and died that evening in Paris at age 52, leaving the throne to Francis I.

Evangelista Torricelli

Birth date: October 14, 1608

Death date: October 24, 1647

Age: 39

Evangelista Torricelli was an Italian physicist and mathematician, remembered above all for inventing the mercury barometer and for work that helped clarify air pressure, motion, optics, and early ideas related to calculus. A pupil of Benedetto Castelli and later connected with Galileo’s circle in Florence, he became one of the sharpest scientific minds of seventeenth-century Italy. His career was brief: in October 1647 he died in Florence after a fever, most likely typhoid, only ten days after turning 39.

Mata Hari

Birth date: August 6, 1876

Death date: October 14, 1917

Age: 41

Mata Hari, born Margaretha Geertruida Zelle in the Netherlands, became one of early twentieth-century Europe’s most famous exotic dancers and courtesans, cultivating a dramatic stage persona that fascinated Parisian society. During World War I, her travels and relationships with officers drew suspicion, and she was convicted by France of spying for Germany. Her guilt remains debated, but she was executed by firing squad at Vincennes on 15 October 1917, aged 41.

Andreas Vesalius

Birth date: December 30, 1514

Death date: October 14, 1564

Age: 49

Andreas Vesalius was a Flemish anatomist and physician whose 1543 masterpiece De humani corporis fabrica transformed the study of the human body by grounding anatomy in direct dissection rather than inherited Galenic authority. He taught at Padua and later served the imperial court. In 1564, after a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, he became ill or was stranded during the return voyage and died on the Greek island of Zakynthos at the age of 49.

Death date: July 9, 1584

Age: 51

William the Silent, or William I, Prince of Orange, was the leading nobleman of the Dutch Revolt against Spanish Habsburg rule and a central founder of the Orange-Nassau line. Remembered in the Netherlands as the Father of the Fatherland, he helped set the political course that eventually led to Dutch independence. After Philip II declared him an outlaw and placed a reward on his head, William was shot in Delft by Balthasar Gérard on 10 July 1584.

Simone Weil

Birth date: February 2, 1909

Death date: August 23, 1943

Age: 34

Simone Weil was a French philosopher, mystic, teacher, writer, and political activist whose short life left a lasting mark on political thought, religious philosophy, and ethics. Born in Paris to a secular Jewish family, she taught, supported labor movements, worked in factories to understand working-class life, and briefly joined anti-fascist forces during the Spanish Civil War. During World War II she worked with the Free French in Britain. Already weakened by illness, tuberculosis, and severe self-denial, she died in Ashford, Kent, from cardiac failure linked to poor health and restricted eating, aged 34.

Ryūnosuke Akutagawa

Birth date: February 29, 1892

Death date: July 23, 1927

Age: 35

Ryūnosuke Akutagawa was a Japanese writer of the Taishō period, celebrated for sharply crafted short stories such as Rashōmon, In a Grove, The Nose, and Hell Screen. Often called a defining figure of the modern Japanese short story, he gave his name to Japan’s prestigious Akutagawa Prize. In his final years he struggled with anxiety, fragile health, and fear of mental illness; on 24 July 1927, he died by suicide from a barbital overdose in Tokyo at the age of 35.

Sándor Petőfi

Birth date: December 31, 1823

Death date: July 30, 1849

Age: 26

Sándor Petőfi was a Hungarian poet, journalist and revolutionary, widely regarded as Hungary's national poet and one of the defining voices of the 1848 Revolution. His poem Nemzeti dal ('National Song') became a symbol of Hungarian independence, and his vivid, direct style made him one of the most influential literary figures in 19th-century Hungary. He disappeared during the Battle of Segesvár on 31 July 1849 while serving with the revolutionary forces; he is generally believed to have been killed there, although his body was never conclusively identified.

Dzhokhar Dudayev

Birth date: February 14, 1944

Death date: April 20, 1996

Age: 52
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Dzhokhar Dudayev is highly controversial because he was a central leader of Chechen separatism and wartime resistance against Russia. Supporters view him as an independence leader, while critics associate his rule and movement with armed conflict, political instability, nationalism, and the violence of the First Chechen War.

Dzhokhar Dudayev was a Chechen military officer, politician, and former Soviet Air Force major general who became the first president of the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria in 1991. A central figure in the Chechen independence movement, he led resistance during the First Chechen War. He was assassinated on 21 April 1996, reportedly after Russian forces located his satellite phone signal and struck him with guided missiles.

Birth date: January 18, 1943

Death date: October 3, 1970

Age: 27

Janis Joplin was an American singer and songwriter whose raw, powerful voice made her one of the defining performers of 1960s rock and blues. She rose to fame with Big Brother and the Holding Company, stunned audiences at Monterey Pop, later played Woodstock, and left classics such as "Piece of My Heart" and "Me and Bobby McGee." Modest Petrovich Mussorgsky

Birth date: March 20, 1839

Death date: March 27, 1881

Age: 42

Modest Petrovich Mussorgsky was a Russian Romantic composer and a member of The Five, the circle that sought a distinctly Russian musical voice. He is best remembered for Boris Godunov, Night on Bald Mountain, and Pictures at an Exhibition, works admired for their bold realism, dramatic instinct, and national color. His later life was marked by poverty, unfinished projects, heavy drinking, seizures, and delirium tremens; he died in Saint Petersburg shortly after his 42nd birthday, with sources linking his final collapse to alcoholism and heart failure.

Joseph II, Holy Roman Emperor

Birth date: March 12, 1741

Death date: February 19, 1790

Age: 48

Joseph II was Holy Roman Emperor from 1765 and sole ruler of the Habsburg Monarchy from 1780, remembered as one of Europe’s most energetic enlightened absolutists. He pushed reforms in religion, law, education, administration, serfdom, and state centralization, often faster than his empire could absorb. His final years were clouded by war, resistance in Hungary and the Austrian Netherlands, and the rollback of several reforms. Already seriously ill after returning to Vienna, he suffered worsening fever, coughing, breathing problems, and chest pain, probably linked to pulmonary tuberculosis, and died in Vienna at age 48.

Christian Doppler

Birth date: November 28, 1803

Death date: March 16, 1853

Age: 49

Christian Andreas Doppler was an Austrian mathematician and physicist whose name became attached to one of the most familiar ideas in wave science: the Doppler effect, the change in observed frequency caused by motion between source and observer. Born in Salzburg, he worked in Prague and Vienna and influenced physics, astronomy, acoustics, and later medical imaging. His final years were marked by worsening chest and lung problems, probably tuberculosis; seeking a gentler climate, he went to Venice, where he died on 1853-03-17 at age 49.

Jacques Brel

Birth date: April 7, 1929

Death date: October 8, 1978

Age: 49

Jacques Brel was a Belgian singer-songwriter, actor, and director whose intense, theatrical chansons made him one of the defining voices of French-language popular music. Songs such as “Ne me quitte pas” and “Amsterdam” helped his work travel far beyond Belgium and France, influencing generations of performers. After years of illness, including lung cancer, he was hospitalized near Paris and died in Bobigny on 9 October 1978, widely reported as the result of a pulmonary embolism. He was 49 and was later buried in the Marquesas Islands.

Death date: May 22, 1498

Girolamo Savonarola was an Italian Dominican friar, preacher, reformer, and briefly the dominant political voice in Florence after the Medici were expelled in 1494. Famous for his fiery sermons against corruption, luxury, and secular culture, he inspired moral campaigns including the “bonfires of the vanities.” His conflict with Pope Alexander VI ended in excommunication, arrest, torture, and trial; on 23 May 1498 he was hanged and his body burned in Florence’s Piazza della Signoria.

Birth date: May 31, 1268

Death date: November 28, 1314

Age: 46

Philip IV of France, known as Philip the Fair, ruled France from 1285 to 1314 and also governed Navarre through his marriage to Joan I. A forceful Capetian monarch, he strengthened royal administration, challenged nobles and clergy, clashed with Pope Boniface VIII, expelled the Jews from France, and destroyed the Knights Templar. In 1314 he suffered a stroke during a hunt near Pont-Sainte-Maxence and died a few weeks later at Fontainebleau, aged 46.

Age: 52

Al-Shafi'i, born Abu Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafi'i, was a major Muslim jurist, hadith scholar and theologian whose teachings gave rise to the Shafi'i school of Sunni Islamic law. Born in Gaza and raised in Mecca, he studied and taught across the Islamic world, including Medina, Baghdad and Egypt, and is closely associated with early systematic writing on legal theory through al-Risala. He died in al-Fustat, Egypt, on 20 January 820 at about 52; later reports disagree on the cause, mentioning chronic illness and a disputed story of an attack after a legal dispute.

He died at age 44 on 4 September 2006 while filming an underwater documentary at the Great Barrier Reef, after a stingray barb pierced his chest, causing fatal injury.

Chadwick Aaron Boseman was an American actor and playwright whose calm intensity and sense of purpose made him one of the defining screen figures of his generation. After studying directing at Howard University, he broke through portraying Jackie Robinson in 42, then played James Brown in Get on Up and Thurgood Marshall in Marshall. He became internationally famous as T’Challa, the Black Panther, in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, bringing dignity, charisma, and cultural weight to a landmark superhero role. Boseman died in Los Angeles on August 28, 2020, at age 43, after a private four-year battle with colon cancer that he had kept from the public while continuing to work.

Death date: July 16, 1762

Peter III of Russia, born Karl Peter Ulrich of Schleswig-Holstein-Gottorp, was the grandson of Peter the Great and briefly ruled as Emperor of Russia in 1762. Raised between German and Russian dynastic worlds, he inherited Holstein-Gottorp and was chosen as heir by Empress Elizabeth. His short reign brought reforms, but his admiration for Prussia and reversal of Russian gains in the Seven Years’ War made him deeply unpopular among powerful elites. After only about six months on the throne, he was overthrown in a palace coup led by supporters of his wife, Catherine II. He was taken to Ropsha and died soon afterward under murky circumstances, officially explained as illness but widely suspected to have involved violence.

Ismail I, also known as Shah Ismail I, was the founder of the Safavid dynasty and the first shah of Safavid Iran, ruling from 1501 to 1524. He unified much of Iran, made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, and became an important patron and poet under the pen name Khatai. Commodus was a Roman emperor, the son of Marcus Aurelius, who ruled first as co-emperor and then alone from 180 to 192. His reign is often remembered as a turning point after the stability of the Pax Romana, marked by court intrigue, autocratic rule, and his notorious public performances as a gladiator. In late 192, after a conspiracy formed around members of his inner circle, he was first poisoned unsuccessfully and then strangled by the wrestler Narcissus, dying in Rome at the age of 31.

Age: 43

Carl Wilhelm Scheele was a German-Swedish pharmaceutical chemist whose experimental skill made him one of the most productive chemical discoverers of the eighteenth century. He independently discovered oxygen before Joseph Priestley published, identified chlorine, and helped reveal substances connected with molybdenum, tungsten, barium, manganese, and many organic and inorganic acids. He worked mainly as a pharmacist rather than as a university professor, which partly explains why his fame lagged behind his achievements. Scheele died in Köping on 21 May 1786 at the age of 43, after years of dangerous laboratory exposure; contemporary and later accounts often connect his decline with poisoning from toxic substances such as mercury, arsenic, lead compounds, cyanides, and acids.

Carl XII of Sweden

Birth date: June 26, 1682

Death date: December 10, 1718

Age: 36

Charles XII of Sweden, also known as Karl XII or Carolus Rex, was the Swedish king from 1697 to 1718 and one of the most famous warrior-monarchs of the Great Northern War. He inherited the throne as a teenager, defeated major enemies early in his reign, and became closely associated with Sweden’s last great-power era. His Russian campaign ended disastrously after Poltava, weakening the Swedish Empire. He died aged 36 during the siege of Fredriksten in Norway, when a projectile struck him in the head; modern research suggests enemy-fired iron grapeshot was the likely cause.

Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg

Birth date: November 14, 1907

Death date: July 20, 1944

Age: 36

Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg was a German army officer and aristocrat who became one of the most important figures in the military resistance to Nazism. A decorated staff officer, he served in several major campaigns of the Second World War before turning decisively against Hitler’s regime. On 20 July 1944, he placed a bomb at Hitler’s Wolf’s Lair headquarters as part of Operation Valkyrie. The assassination failed, and Stauffenberg was arrested and executed in Berlin shortly after midnight, dying at the age of 36.

Viktor Tsoi was a Soviet singer-songwriter, actor, and the iconic co-founder and frontman of Kino, the band that helped define late-Soviet rock. Born in Leningrad to a Russian mother and a Koryo-saram father, he became one of the most influential voices in Russian-language music; in August 1990, while in Latvia after a major concert period and working on new material, he died at 28 in a road collision when his car crossed into oncoming traffic.

Edward II of England

Birth date: April 24, 1284

Death date: September 20, 1327

Age: 43

Edward II of England was a Plantagenet king who ruled from 1307 until his deposition in 1327. His reign was marked by conflict with powerful barons, controversy over royal favourites such as Piers Gaveston and Hugh Despenser the Younger, and a disastrous defeat by Robert the Bruce at Bannockburn. After Queen Isabella and Roger Mortimer invaded England, Edward was forced to abdicate in favour of his son, Edward III. He died at Berkeley Castle on 21 September 1327, aged 43, probably murdered while in captivity.

Marcus Junius Brutus

Birth date: May 31, 85 BCE

Death date: October 22, 42 BCE

Age: 43

Marcus Junius Brutus was a Roman politician, orator, and senator of the late Republic, remembered above all as one of the principal conspirators in the assassination of Julius Caesar in 44 BCE. Once pardoned and favored by Caesar, Brutus later cast himself as a defender of republican liberty against dictatorship. After Caesar’s murder, he and Cassius led the republican forces against Mark Antony and Octavian. Defeated at Philippi in 42 BCE, Brutus died by suicide near the battlefield, aged about 43.

Stephen II

Death date: April 25, 757

Age: 43

Pope Stephen II was bishop of Rome from 752 to 757 and a pivotal figure in the shift from Byzantine to Frankish influence over the papacy. Facing Lombard pressure on Rome, he appealed to Pepin the Short, whose military support and land grants helped lay the foundations of the Papal States. Stephen died in Rome on 26 April 757, probably aged about 43, and was succeeded by his brother Paul I.

Philip the Arab, born Marcus Julius Philippus, was Roman emperor from 244 to 249 and came from Arabia Petraea, in the region of modern Syria. A former praetorian prefect, he rose to power after Gordian III’s death, made peace with the Sasanian Empire, and presided over Rome’s millennium celebrations in 248. His final year was marked by military unrest and the rise of Decius; Philip was killed in September 249 during or shortly after the Battle of Verona.

Philip III of Spain, also Philip II of Portugal, was a Habsburg king whose reign covered the height of the Iberian Union and much of Spain's global imperial power. Age: 36

Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot was a French military engineer and physicist whose 1824 work on heat engines laid the conceptual foundation for thermodynamics and later influenced Kelvin and Clausius. Though little celebrated in his lifetime, he became known as the father of thermodynamics. He died young, at 36, during the 1832 cholera epidemic; fear of contamination led to the loss of many of his papers.

Báb

Birth date: October 19, 1819

Death date: July 8, 1850

Age: 30

The Báb, born Siyyid ʻAlí Muḥammad Shírází, was an Iranian merchant and religious leader who founded Bábism in 1844 and became a central forerunner figure in the Baháʼí Faith. His writings announced a new religious dispensation, emphasized spiritual renewal, and anticipated a greater promised figure later identified by Baháʼís as Baháʼu'lláh. His movement rapidly attracted followers and alarmed Qajar authorities and clerics. After imprisonment and interrogation, he was executed by firing squad in Tabriz on 9 July 1850, dying at the age of 30.

Elagabalus

Birth date: March 19, 203

Death date: March 10, 222

Age: 18
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Elagabalus is controversial because ancient sources portray his reign as scandalous, especially for religious disruption, conflict with Roman elites, sexual allegations, and gender-related stories. Many of those accounts were written by hostile elite authors, so modern historians treat parts of the scandal tradition cautiously.

Elagabalus was a teenage Roman emperor of the Severan dynasty who ruled from 218 to 222 CE after rising from his role as priest of the sun god Elagabal in Emesa. His reign became famous for religious upheaval, court scandal, and conflict with Rome’s political elite; in March 222 he was assassinated by the Praetorian Guard during a coup and replaced by Severus Alexander.

Guy Fawkes

Birth date: April 12, 1570

Death date: January 30, 1606

Age: 35
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Guy Fawkes was part of the Gunpowder Plot, a conspiracy to blow up Parliament and kill King James I. He is remembered both as a symbol of resistance and as a participant in an attempted mass-casualty political assassination.

Guy Fawkes, also known as Guido Fawkes, was an English soldier and Catholic conspirator best remembered for his role in the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, a failed attempt to blow up the House of Lords and kill King James I. Born in York, he fought for Catholic Spain before joining Robert Catesby's conspiracy. After being discovered guarding barrels of gunpowder beneath Parliament, he was tortured, tried for high treason, and sentenced to be hanged, drawn and quartered. On 31 January 1606, he died at the gallows in Westminster, reportedly breaking his neck and avoiding the full brutality of the sentence.

Georges Seurat

Birth date: December 1, 1859

Death date: March 28, 1891

Age: 31

Georges Seurat was a French Post-Impressionist painter whose precise, luminous technique helped launch Neo-Impressionism and made pointillism famous. His masterpiece A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte changed the course of modern painting with its disciplined dots of color and carefully structured calm. He died in Paris at only 31 after a brief illness; the exact cause remains uncertain, with infectious angina, meningitis, pneumonia, and diphtheria all cited by later sources.

Edward IV of England

Birth date: April 27, 1442

Death date: April 8, 1483

Age: 40

Edward IV was the first Yorkist king of England and one of the central rulers of the Wars of the Roses. He seized the throne from Henry VI in 1461, lost it briefly in 1470, and regained it after decisive victories at Barnet and Tewkesbury in 1471. His later reign was comparatively stable, though shaped by dynastic tension and the political consequences of his marriage to Elizabeth Woodville. He fell seriously ill around Easter 1483 and died at Westminster on 9 April 1483, aged 40; his young son Edward V succeeded him but was soon displaced by Richard III.

Alexander Vasilyevich Kolchak was a Russian admiral, Arctic explorer, oceanographer, and one of the central leaders of the anti-Bolshevik White movement during the Russian Civil War. His government collapsed after military defeats and loss of support. Birth date: September 8, 384

Death date: August 14, 423

Age: 38

Honorius, born Flavius Honorius, was Western Roman emperor during one of the empire’s most unstable periods. The younger son of Theodosius I, he inherited the western half of the Roman world while his brother Arcadius ruled the east. His reign is remembered for court politics, dependence on powerful generals such as Stilicho, frontier collapse, and the Visigothic sack of Rome in 410. Honorius died at Ravenna from edema on 15 August 423 at age 38, leaving no direct heir and opening a brief succession crisis.

Birth date: December 31, 972

Death date: February 17, 999

Age: 27

Pope Gregory V, born Bruno of Carinthia, was the first German pope and ruled the Church from 996 to 999 during one of the most turbulent moments of the late 10th century. Chosen by his cousin, Emperor Otto III, he crowned Otto as Holy Roman Emperor, faced revolt in Rome, was driven out by enemies who backed the antipope John XVI, and returned after imperial intervention. He died suddenly in Rome in 999, probably of malaria though the exact cause remains uncertain, at about 27 years old.

Did you know:

For most of history, a drink of water was also a gamble. Rivers, wells, and town pumps could carry sewage-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid. In the United States, typhoid fever was about 100 cases per 100,000 people in 1900; after water treatment, sanitation, and disinfection spread, it fell to 33.8 by 1920 and 0.1 by 2006. A glass of boring tap water may be one of the greatest inventions in history.

The humbling part is that this is not ancient history everywhere. WHO estimates that around 1 million people still die each year from diarrhoea linked to unsafe drinking water, sanitation, and hand hygiene. So when someone in a modern city turns a tap, showers, brushes teeth, and flushes a toilet without thinking, they are living inside a public-health miracle.
